entries.prompt: Part 1 — The harvest and the hail
entries.answer: Lencho is a poor farmer who lives with his family in a solitary house on the crest of a low hill in the valley. His field of ripe corn promises a good harvest, and he is sure that God is looking at his crops with satisfaction, just as he gazes at his fields in the sky. Lencho compares his cornfield to a field of flowers because of the golden colour of the ripe corn and the tall plants bowing to the wind. He is a simple, hardworking man whose only hope of survival depends entirely on this harvest. One night, however, his hopes are crushed: a hailstorm destroys the whole crop in barely an hour. With the leaves gone and the plants covered in frozen pearls of ice, Lencho knows there will be no harvest that year, and he fears that he and his family will go hungry through the winter.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The letter to God
entries.answer: Lencho has strong faith in God. He believes that God sees everything, even what a man as poor as he is thinking about. Although his family is starving and his job in the field is finished, his heart does not lose hope. On the following Sunday he writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos, explaining that he needs the money to sow his field again and to live until the new crop comes. He posts the letter at the post office, addressing it simply "To God". The postman and the postmaster, a fat and amiable fellow, laugh at the idea at first. But the postmaster soon becomes serious and admires Lencho's unshakable faith, marvelling that a man who can see the "nothing but a black dot above the green field" should still believe so firmly in God.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The reply and its cost
entries.answer: The postmaster decides not to break Lencho's faith. He collects money from his employees, contributes part of his own salary, and manages to gather seventy pesos, which he sends in an envelope addressed to Lencho. He signs the letter simply "God". When Lencho receives the letter, he is not surprised that God has replied, but he becomes angry on counting the money, because it is not the hundred pesos he had asked for. Convinced that the post-office employees have stolen the rest, he writes another letter to God demanding that the missing thirty pesos be sent to him directly, and he tells God not to send the money by mail because "the post office employees are a bunch of crooks".

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The irony of the ending
entries.answer: The story ends with the postmaster laughing heartily but feeling deeply touched by Lencho's blind faith. When the postman hands him Lencho's second letter, the postmaster reads it and understands the irony: the man who has been helped by the post office employees calls them crooks, while the postmaster himself has given part of his salary to help this very farmer. The postmaster's reaction — laughing until tears come to his eyes — is the central irony of the story. Lencho's faith in God remains unshaken even when he doubts the honesty of men, which is exactly what the postmaster admires and what makes him reluctant to reveal the truth.

entries.prompt: Faith in God
entries.answer: The central theme of the story is Lencho's unshakable faith in God. Lencho is an illiterate farmer, yet his trust in God is absolute: he writes to God as one would write to a friend, he is not surprised that God answers his letter, and even when the money is short he does not doubt God's honesty — he only doubts the honesty of men. The postmaster, a worldly man, is moved by this faith and does everything in his power to preserve it, showing that simple faith can touch even those who do not share it.

entries.prompt: Human kindness and the unseen good
entries.answer: The theme of human kindness runs through the story: the postmaster and his employees, though they laugh at Lencho's letter, quietly collect seventy pesos and send it as if it came from God. They perform an act of charity without any expectation of gratitude. The irony is that the very people who help Lencho are the ones he accuses of being "a bunch of crooks". This contrast between human goodness and human suspicion shows how often kindness goes unrecognised.

entries.prompt: The irony of fate and appearance
entries.answer: The story is built on dramatic irony. The reader knows that the money came from the postmaster and his staff, while Lencho believes it came from God and that the employees are thieves. Lencho's letter praising God while insulting his actual benefactors is deeply ironic. The title itself prepares us for this irony: a letter to God becomes a letter that exposes the gap between blind faith and everyday reality.

entries.prompt: Lencho
entries.answer: Lencho is a poor, hardworking farmer who lives alone with his family on a hill. He is an illiterate, simple man whose entire life depends on his cornfield. His strongest trait is his extraordinary faith in God: he writes a letter to God without hesitation, expecting a reply, and is not surprised when one comes. He is trusting to the point of innocence, yet also practical — he counts the money and insists that the rest be sent. His famous complaint that the post office employees are "a bunch of crooks" reveals a man who trusts God absolutely but has little faith in men, and it is this very combination that makes him both admirable and comical.

entries.prompt: The postmaster
entries.answer: The postmaster is a fat, amiable fellow who first laughs at the idea of a letter addressed to God, but is soon deeply impressed by Lencho's faith. He is kind-hearted and generous: he collects money from his colleagues, gives part of his own salary, and sends seventy pesos to a stranger so as not to break that faith. His emotional response — laughing at the second letter even as tears come to his eyes — shows his humanity. He represents the unseen kindness of ordinary people and the quiet good that Lencho fails to recognise.

entries.prompt: The postman and the post office employees
entries.answer: The post office employees are the unseen heroes of the story. When the postmaster shares Lencho's letter with them, they laugh — but they also give generously: each contributes part of his salary, and the postmaster himself adds a portion of his own, so that seventy pesos can be sent to a complete stranger. Their kindness is entirely anonymous; Lencho never knows them and even denounces them as crooks. They represent the ordinary goodness in everyday people — the quiet charity that asks for no recognition, which is the story's most moving irony.

entries.prompt: Faith and hope in adversity
entries.answer: Lencho teaches us that faith can be a source of strength in the hardest times. When his entire crop is destroyed, he does not despair but turns to God with complete trust. The value of hope is that it keeps a person working and believing even when circumstances seem hopeless.

entries.prompt: Honesty and gratitude
entries.answer: The story raises the value of honesty and gratitude. The postmaster and his employees act honestly and generously, yet Lencho, because he cannot see who his real benefactor is, responds with suspicion and ingratitude. The lesson is that we should recognise and be grateful for the kindness of the people around us, not take it for granted.

entries.prompt: Why did Lencho compare his ripe cornfield to a field of flowers?
entries.answer: Lencho compared his cornfield to a field of flowers because the ripe corn shone golden in the sunlight and the tall plants, bending in the wind, resembled flowers. To him the field was a source of beauty as well as livelihood.

entries.prompt: What happened to Lencho's crop in one night?
entries.answer: A violent hailstorm destroyed Lencho's entire crop in a single night. The rain turned into large hailstones that fell like new silver coins, and within an hour the field was white with ice and the leaves of the corn plants were completely destroyed.

entries.prompt: How much money did Lencho ask for, and why?
entries.answer: Lencho asked for one hundred pesos. He needed the money to sow his field again and to feed his family until the new crop came, because the hailstorm had ruined his only source of income for the year.

entries.prompt: Why was Lencho not surprised to receive a reply from God?
entries.answer: Lencho was not surprised because he had complete faith in God. He believed that God always answered the prayers of those who trusted him, and he was sure that God would not disappoint a poor man who had asked for help so sincerely.

entries.prompt: Why was Lencho angry when he counted the money?
entries.answer: Lencho was angry because the envelope contained only seventy pesos instead of the hundred he had asked for. He was convinced that God could not have made a mistake, so the thirty pesos must have been stolen by the post office employees.

entries.prompt: How did the postmaster collect the money for Lencho?
entries.answer: The postmaster collected money from his employees, who were willing to contribute to an act of charity, and he gave part of his own salary as well. In this way he gathered seventy pesos and sent them to Lencho in an envelope addressed to God.

entries.prompt: What did Lencho write in his second letter to God?
entries.answer: In his second letter Lencho demanded the thirty pesos that were missing, and he asked God not to send the money by mail because the post office employees were, in his words, "a bunch of crooks".

entries.prompt: How did the postmaster react to Lencho's second letter?
entries.answer: The postmaster laughed heartily when he read the letter, but there were tears of emotion in his eyes. He was touched by Lencho's unshakable faith in God and by the irony that the man he had helped now called his benefactors thieves.

entries.prompt: Describe the irony in the story "A Letter to God".
entries.answer: The central irony of the story is that Lencho's faith in God is absolute while his faith in men is nil. The postmaster and his employees secretly collect seventy pesos to help the poor farmer and send it in God's name, yet Lencho accuses exactly these benefactors of stealing thirty pesos. The postmaster's reaction — laughing with tears in his eyes — captures this irony perfectly: he is amused at Lencho's innocence but also moved by a faith so strong that it survives even when the money is short. Thus the story shows that people often fail to recognise the goodness of those around them while trusting completely in what they cannot see.

entries.prompt: What does the story tell us about the value of faith and the nature of human kindness?
entries.answer: The story shows that faith gives a person strength and hope in the face of disaster. Lencho's trust in God keeps him from despair when his crop is destroyed, and his certainty that God will answer his letter gives him the courage to plan again. At the same time, the story celebrates human kindness: the postmaster and his staff give their own money to help a stranger, and the postmaster works hard to protect Lencho's faith rather than mock it. The irony is that this kindness goes unacknowledged, which teaches us that true charity is performed without expectation of gratitude, and that we should value the goodness of the people around us.

entries.prompt: Why did Lencho call the post office employees "a bunch of crooks"? Was he justified?
entries.answer: Lencho called the post office employees crooks because he received seventy pesos instead of the hundred he had asked for, and he was certain that God could not have made a mistake. In his simple logic, if God sent the money, and the amount was short, then someone between God and him must have taken it — and that someone had to be the post office employees. He was not justified, because the employees had actually helped him generously: the postmaster had collected the seventy pesos from his own and his colleagues' pockets. The reader knows the truth, so Lencho's accusation is an example of dramatic irony — he is accusing the very people who rescued his family.

entries.prompt: How does Lencho's character reveal the contrast between faith in God and faith in man?
entries.answer: Lencho's character is built on this contrast. His faith in God is childlike and complete: he writes to God without hesitation, waits for a reply as a matter of course, and is not surprised when the letter arrives. But his faith in man is almost non-existent — the moment the money falls short, he assumes the employees are thieves. This contrast is deliberate: the author shows that it is easier for a simple man to trust an unseen God than the visible men around him. Yet ironically, it is men — the postmaster and his staff — who actually answer his prayer, while God remains unseen. Through Lencho, the story suggests that human goodness and divine faith are connected, and that both deserve our trust.

entries.prompt: Value question: What lesson about gratitude does the story teach us?
entries.answer: The story teaches us that we should recognise and be grateful for the kindness of others. The postmaster and his employees gave their own hard-earned money to help Lencho without expecting any thanks, yet Lencho responded by insulting them. His blindness to their generosity shows how easily we take help for granted and accuse the very people who serve us. The lesson is that gratitude is a virtue: before we complain about what we did not receive, we should acknowledge the good that others have already done for us, often quietly and anonymously.

entries.prompt: The postmaster says he admires Lencho's faith. Do you think the postmaster's act was right? Give reasons.
entries.answer: Yes, the postmaster's act was right because it protected the faith of a desperate, innocent man at a moment when he had lost everything. By collecting money and sending it as a reply from God, the postmaster gave Lencho the means to sow his field again and the hope to continue. Some may argue that the deception was wrong, but the postmaster's intention was pure charity, and he even refused to reveal the truth later because he did not want to destroy Lencho's trust in God. The story suggests that kindness, even when it hides behind a small lie, is a form of goodness.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — Horace Danby
entries.answer: Horace Danby was fifty years old, and everyone in the town thought he was a good, honest man — he ran a locksmith business, worked hard and was so gentle that he would never harm a fly. But the truth was that Horace was not really honest: he burgled a safe every year, stealing just enough to buy the rare, expensive books he loved. He had a perfect plan: he studied the family for a fortnight, knew their habits, and broke in only when the house would be empty. This year he had targeted the house of a rich man who lived in the country, a house with a safe containing precious stones.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The surprise in the house
entries.answer: Horace got to the house as planned. He wore gloves and was careful not to leave fingerprints. Inside, he discovered a small safe that was easy to open — he had brought tools for a more difficult job. Just as he was opening the safe, a voice startled him: a young woman stood in the doorway, watching him. She said she was the wife of the rich man, and that she was too frightened to call the police because of her husband's temper — he would be very angry if he knew she was involved in a burglary. She asked Horace to open the safe and steal from it, but to give her all the money, and to leave her only with the jewels.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The betrayal
entries.answer: Horace, surprised by her calm, agreed. He opened the safe, took the jewels and handed them to her. She asked how he would escape the dog, and he explained his plan — the dog knew him because he had fed it on earlier visits. Before leaving, the woman asked him to tie her up and gag her, so that the police would believe she too was a victim. Horace did so, then escaped, pleased that he had done the job without violence. He even imagined the woman would keep his secret.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The arrest
entries.answer: Three days later, Horace was arrested. The police had found his fingerprints in the house — on the door and on the safe. They showed him a photo of the real wife of the owner: she was a large, middle-aged woman, nothing like the young woman he had met. Horace realised he had been tricked. The young woman was another thief, who had simply appeared and taken the jewels. She had even stolen his gloves by playing on his kindness, asking him to tie her up so that his fingerprints would remain in the house. Horace, the "gentle" burglar who trusted a fellow thief, was caught because of that trust. He tells the police that the woman is a clever one — so clever that he would never tell anyone, not even to save himself, for he "could not describe her" — a quiet admission of his defeat.

entries.prompt: The bitter irony of trust
entries.answer: The central theme is the irony of trust. Horace trusts the young woman's story completely — her claim to be the owner's wife, her fear of her husband's temper, her request for help — and that trust is his undoing. The title "A Question of Trust" is deeply ironic: the man whose profession is betrayal is himself betrayed, and the "gentle" thief is caught because he was too trusting of the wrong person.

entries.prompt: Crime never pays
entries.answer: The story illustrates that crime never pays, in the deepest sense. Horace's "harmless" yearly thefts — enough for his beloved books — lead him to a bigger job, where he is outwitted by a cleverer criminal and arrested. The story also shows that even the "gentle" criminal is a criminal: his trustworthiness, kindness and love of books do not excuse his burglaries, and in the end he pays for them.

entries.prompt: Horace Danby
entries.answer: Horace Danby is a fifty-year-old locksmith with an excellent reputation: the town believes him gentle, honest and hard-working. In truth he is a secret, methodical burglar who steals once a year, just enough to buy rare books — his one passion. He is careful, experienced and proud of his planning, yet he is also naive in a human way: he is moved by the young woman's story, treats her gallantly, and trusts her completely. That gallantry and trust are his downfall — he is betrayed, framed and arrested. Horace's tragedy is that his one genuinely good quality, trust, is exactly what destroys him. He remains a likeable figure, which makes the irony of his fate sharper.

entries.prompt: The young woman
entries.answer: The young woman is the brilliant villain of the story, a professional thief disguised as the rich man's wife. She is cool, quick-witted and utterly convincing: she appears in the doorway, plays on Horace's chivalry with her story of a violent husband, persuades him to open the safe, takes the jewels, asks him to tie her up — and even takes his gloves, telling him the dog would not know her scent. When the police come, they find only Horace's fingerprints. She vanishes without a trace, and Horace, impressed despite himself, refuses to describe her — "a clever one" indeed. She is the mirror image of Horace: a thief who trusts no one and wins.

entries.prompt: The real wife and the police
entries.answer: The real wife of the owner is a large, middle-aged woman whose photo in the newspaper shatters Horace's story. The police, efficient and thorough, discover Horace's fingerprints at the scene and piece together the truth: the young woman had taken his gloves, so his prints were everywhere, and the jewels were never recovered. The wife and the police represent the ordinary world that Horace's double life finally collides with — impersonal, patient and ultimately more successful than the cleverest burglar.

entries.prompt: Honesty and reputation
entries.answer: The story shows that a good reputation must be backed by true honesty. Horace was "good" in everyone's eyes yet lived a double life, and his secret crime destroyed him. The lesson is that character is what we do when no one is watching; trust is precious, and both giving and earning it require integrity.

entries.prompt: Be careful whom you trust
entries.answer: The story also warns about misplaced trust. Horace's trust in the stranger was instant and complete, and it cost him his freedom. The lesson is not cynicism but discernment: kindness and gallantry are admirable, but they must be balanced with judgment, because not everyone who seems helpless deserves our confidence.

entries.prompt: Who was Horace Danby?
entries.answer: Horace Danby was a fifty-year-old locksmith, well respected in his town, who secretly committed one burglary a year to buy rare books.

entries.prompt: Why did Horace commit burglaries?
entries.answer: He stole only what he needed to buy the rare, expensive books he loved — his one weakness.

entries.prompt: What was Horace's usual method?
entries.answer: He studied the family of his target for a fortnight, learned their habits, and broke in only when the house would be empty.

entries.prompt: Who did Horace meet inside the house?
entries.answer: A young woman who claimed to be the owner's wife and said she was too frightened of her husband's temper to call the police.

entries.prompt: What did the young woman ask Horace to do?
entries.answer: She asked him to open the safe, give her all the money, leave her the jewels, and tie her up so the police would think her a victim too.

entries.prompt: How was Horace caught?
entries.answer: His fingerprints were found in the house — the young woman had taken his gloves, so his prints remained on the door and safe.

entries.prompt: Who was the young woman really?
entries.answer: She was another thief, who had tricked Horace into opening the safe and then framed him, escaping with the jewels.

entries.prompt: Why did Horace refuse to describe the woman?
entries.answer: He admired her cleverness so much that he would not describe her, even to save himself — she was, in his words, a clever one.

entries.prompt: Why is the title "A Question of Trust" ironical?
entries.answer: The title is deeply ironical because trust — an admirable quality — is exactly what destroys the burglar. Horace Danby is a criminal who trusts no one in his profession; he works alone, with careful plans and gloves. Yet when the young woman appears with her story, he trusts her completely: her claim to be the owner's wife, her fear of her husband's temper, her request for help. He even behaves gallantly, tying her up at her request. That trust is his undoing — she is a fellow thief who takes the jewels, takes his gloves and leaves his fingerprints behind. The "question of trust" is answered ironically: the man who trusted is arrested, and the woman who trusted no one escapes. Even at the end, Horace's trust is so complete that he refuses to describe her — he cannot bring himself to betray the person who betrayed him.

entries.prompt: Describe the character of Horace Danby. Was he truly good?
entries.answer: Horace Danby was fifty years old, a successful locksmith, gentle and hard-working, and universally considered honest — "he would not even harm a fly." But this goodness was a mask. Every year he planned and executed a burglary, stealing only enough to buy the rare books he loved. He was methodical, patient and proud of his skill, studying his targets for a fortnight. Yet his character had genuine softness: he was moved by the young woman's story, behaved with courtesy, and trusted her absolutely. He was not truly good — theft is theft, whatever the motive — but he was not truly bad either; he was a man with a weakness (books) and a self-deception (that his "gentle" crimes were harmless). The story shows that he paid for his double life: his one honest feeling, trust, became the trap that caught him.

entries.prompt: How did the young woman outwit Horace?
entries.answer: The young woman outwitted Horace at every step. First, she used psychology: instead of screaming or calling the police, she calmly announced herself as the owner's wife and gave a reason to stay silent — her husband's violent temper. This made Horace her accomplice instead of her enemy. Second, she made him do the work: he opened the safe and handed her the jewels, believing he was helping a frightened woman. Third, she secured the evidence: asking him to tie her up, she ensured his prints were on her and on the scene, and by taking his gloves she guaranteed his fingerprints would be found everywhere — while hers would not. Finally, she disappeared cleanly with the jewels, leaving Horace to the police. Her victory was total: she even persuaded him to admire her. Against her intelligence, Horace's careful planning was helpless.

entries.prompt: Value question: What lesson does the story teach about trust and judgment?
entries.answer: The story teaches that trust must be combined with judgment. Horace's downfall was not that he trusted, but that he trusted blindly and instantly — a stranger's story, told at midnight in a stolen house, was accepted without a question. The young woman exploited his gallantry and his belief in his own cleverness. The lesson is twofold. First, for the honest: our good qualities — kindness, trust, generosity — are precisely what dishonest people prey on, so they must be exercised with discernment. Second, for everyone: character is shown in what we do in secret; a reputation for honesty cannot survive a dishonest life. Horace's secret crimes were discovered, and his public goodness counted for nothing. The story's deepest message is that we should be trustworthy ourselves, and careful in whom we place our trust.

entries.prompt: Why does Horace refuse to describe the young woman to the police?
entries.answer: Horace's refusal to describe the young woman is the story's final irony. He tells the police that she was "a clever one" — and that he would never describe her, "not even to save himself." Several motives mingle here. There is grudging admiration: he respects her brilliance, and he is a professional himself. There is also wounded pride: she outwitted him completely, and describing her would be to admit that a simple story fooled him. And there may be a strange loyalty: in the strange morality of thieves, she was his companion in crime, and informing on her would be a final, unbearable humiliation. The refusal completes the title's irony — the victim of misplaced trust remains, to the end, trusting: he will not betray the one person who betrayed him.

entries.prompt: Stanza-wise meaning
entries.answer: The poem contrasts the tiger's life in the zoo with the life he should be living in the wild. In the cage, the tiger walks a few steps back and forth on "pads of velvet quiet", hiding his anger in the silence of his confinement; he stares at the stars with brilliant eyes but cannot see the jungle. The poet then imagines the tiger in his natural home: lurking in the shadow of long grass near the river, snarling around houses at the jungle's edge, terrorising the villagers, and sliding through the tall grass at night to drink from the waterhole. In the final stanza, the poet returns to the zoo: the tiger paces behind the bars, his strength of "quiet rage" locked away, watching the patrolling cars through the night.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves between two worlds: the cage and the jungle. It opens with the tiger in the zoo — confined, pacing, silent — and then imagines the same tiger in the wild, where he should be: hunting, stalking, terrorising, drinking from the waterhole. The movement is a constant contrast between freedom and captivity, power and powerlessness. The poem ends where it began — the tiger still in his cage, his rage and strength wasted behind bars. The circular structure reinforces the theme: nothing has changed; the tiger remains imprisoned while his true self, the wild predator, can only be imagined.

entries.prompt: Freedom versus captivity
entries.answer: The central theme is the contrast between freedom and captivity. The tiger in the cage is a shadow of himself: his power, beauty and dignity are trapped behind bars. In the wild, he would be a hunter and a terror of the jungle; in the zoo, he is reduced to pacing a few steps. The poem criticises the confinement of wild animals, showing that captivity destroys the very nature of the creature.

entries.prompt: The dignity of wild creatures
entries.answer: The poem celebrates the tiger's natural dignity and strength. In the jungle, the tiger is magnificent — sliding through grass, terrorising villages, drinking from the waterhole. The poem suggests that this wildness is the tiger's true self, and that keeping such a creature in a cage is a cruelty that robs it of its identity. The "quiet rage" of the caged tiger is the suppressed protest of a proud creature against its imprisonment.

entries.prompt: The tiger
entries.answer: The tiger is the subject of the poem, presented through two contrasting portraits. In the cage, he is quiet, restless and angry — pacing on velvet-soft pads, his brilliant eyes fixed on the stars, his rage held in silence. In the poet's imagination, he is a fierce predator: lurking, snarling, terrorising, drinking from the waterhole. The tiger thus stands for all wild animals deprived of freedom, and his "quiet rage" represents the silent suffering of creatures that cannot voice their pain.

entries.prompt: The poet/speaker
entries.answer: The speaker is a compassionate observer who imagines the tiger's inner life. He enters the tiger's mind, picturing what the animal should be doing in the wild, and his imagination is full of longing and sorrow for the imprisoned creature. The speaker's sympathy for the tiger and his criticism of the zoo show a deep concern for animal welfare and a recognition of the dignity of wild life.

entries.prompt: Structure and rhyme
entries.answer: The poem has five stanzas, each of four lines, with a regular rhyme scheme (ABCB) in most stanzas. The regularity of the form gives the poem a controlled, formal quality that matches the controlled world of the zoo, while the variations mirror the tiger's restless pacing. The short, clipped lines of the final stanza ("Near the water hole / Where plump deer pass") echo the careful steps of the caged animal.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone of the poem is sympathetic, contemplative and quietly angry. The poet's pity for the caged tiger is conveyed through gentle, precise images, while his anger at the injustice of captivity is conveyed through the "quiet rage" of the tiger itself. The mood is sombre: the poem's circular structure, returning to the cage at the end, leaves the reader with a sense of sorrow and helplessness — the tiger remains imprisoned, and nothing can free him.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem is rich in visual imagery: the velvet-soft pads, the brilliant eyes, the long grass, the village houses, the waterhole. The tiger itself is a symbol of wildness, freedom and power — and of the suffering caused by their loss. The cage and the bars symbolise confinement and the destruction of nature by civilisation. The stars the tiger sees through the cage symbolise the freedom he can glimpse but never reach, while the jungle scenes symbolise the life he should have had.

entries.prompt: OXYMORON
entries.answer: "Quiet rage" combines two contradictory ideas — silence and fury. The oxymoron captures the tiger's suppressed anger: he is furious but cannot express his fury; his rage is locked inside him, as he is locked inside his cage.

entries.prompt: ALLITERATION
entries.answer: The repetition of consonant sounds, as in "He stalks in his vivid stripes" and "pads of velvet quiet", creates a smooth, gliding rhythm that mimics the tiger's silent movements and adds to the poem's musical quality.

entries.prompt: METAPHOR
entries.answer: "On pads of velvet quiet" is a metaphor comparing the tiger's soft paws to velvet, suggesting both softness and stealth. The metaphor makes the tiger's movements seem luxurious yet deadly, contrasting sharply with the poverty of his cage life.

entries.prompt: PERSONIFICATION
entries.answer: The tiger is given human emotions: he has "quiet rage" and is "ignoring his visitors". By attributing feelings of anger and contempt to the tiger, the poet makes the reader feel the animal's suffering as a fellow being's, deepening the poem's sympathy.

entries.prompt: REPETITION
entries.answer: The word "brilliant" is repeated ("And stares with his brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars") to emphasise the contrast between the tiger's natural brilliance and the darkness of his cage. The repetition highlights how wasted his magnificence is in captivity.

entries.prompt: CONTRAST (CAGE VS JUNGLE)
entries.answer: The poem is structured on the contrast between the cage and the jungle: confinement against freedom, silence against snarling, the patrolling cars against the waterhole. The contrasts make the tragedy of the tiger's captivity vivid, and each image of the wild underlines what has been lost.

entries.prompt: IMAGERY
entries.answer: The poem creates powerful visual images: the pacing tiger behind bars, the velvet-soft paws, the brilliant eyes fixed on stars, the jungle scenes of grass, houses and waterholes. The imagery moves between confinement and freedom, making the tiger's world — and his loss — vividly real to the reader.

entries.prompt: SYMBOLISM
entries.answer: The tiger symbolises wild nature and freedom; the cage and bars symbolise captivity and the domination of nature by humans. The poem as a whole is a symbol of the conflict between civilisation and the natural world, and the tiger's "quiet rage" symbolises the silent suffering of all imprisoned creatures.

entries.prompt: What does the tiger do in his cage?
entries.answer: The tiger stalks back and forth in his cage, taking a few steps between the corners, walking on his soft paws and staring at the stars through the cage with brilliant, angry eyes.

entries.prompt: Where should the tiger be lurking in the wild?
entries.answer: In the wild, the tiger should be lurking in the shadow of long grass near the river, waiting to prey on the deer that come to drink at the waterhole.

entries.prompt: What does the tiger do around houses at the jungle's edge?
entries.answer: In the wild, the tiger would snarl around houses at the jungle's edge, baring his white fangs and claws, terrorising the villagers.

entries.prompt: What is the "quiet rage" of the tiger?
entries.answer: "Quiet rage" is the tiger's suppressed fury at being caged. He is angry at his captivity, but his rage is silent because he cannot express it — an oxymoron that captures his helplessness.

entries.prompt: How does the poet describe the tiger's walk in the cage?
entries.answer: The poet says the tiger stalks in his vivid stripes, taking a few steps of his cage, on pads of velvet quiet, in his quiet rage.

entries.prompt: What does the tiger see through the cage at night?
entries.answer: At night, the tiger stares at the brilliant stars through the cage, and he can see the patrolling cars passing outside the zoo, but he cannot see the jungle he longs for.

entries.prompt: What is the rhyme scheme of the poem?
entries.answer: The poem has a mostly regular rhyme scheme of ABCB in each of its five quatrains, giving it a controlled, formal structure.

entries.prompt: What does the poem criticise?
entries.answer: The poem criticises the confinement of wild animals in zoos, showing that captivity destroys a wild creature's freedom, dignity and natural way of life.

entries.prompt: Explain the contrast between the tiger's life in the cage and his life in the wild.
entries.answer: The poem presents two sharply contrasting portraits of the same tiger. In the cage, he is a prisoner: he paces a few steps between the bars on velvet-soft pads, hides his rage in silence and stares longingly at the stars. His world is confined, artificial and dead — nothing moves but himself, and even his brilliance is wasted. In the wild, he is a king: he lurks in the shadow of long grass near the river, snarls around houses baring his fangs, terrorises the village and slides through the grass to drink at the waterhole among plump deer. The wild tiger is powerful, feared and free; the caged tiger is helpless, ignored and broken. The contrast is the heart of the poem, showing what captivity takes from a wild creature: not just freedom, but its very identity.

entries.prompt: What does the tiger's "quiet rage" tell us about his feelings?
entries.answer: The tiger's "quiet rage" reveals that he is deeply angry at his captivity but powerless to express or act on that anger. The oxymoron "quiet rage" combines two opposites — silence and fury — suggesting an anger so deep that it has turned inward. The tiger cannot roar, attack or escape; he can only pace and stare. His rage is the natural fury of a wild predator whose power has been rendered useless, and its silence makes it more poignant than any roar. The phrase also invites the reader to consider the suffering of zoo animals: behind their calm, beautiful appearance lies a world of suppressed frustration and despair. The tiger's quiet rage is thus a silent protest against the loss of his freedom.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about the treatment of wild animals?
entries.answer: The poem teaches us that wild animals have a right to their natural life, and that keeping them in cages for human entertainment is a form of cruelty. The tiger in the zoo is not living — he is merely existing, pacing a few steps in "quiet rage", his brilliance wasted. The poem shows that an animal's dignity lies in its freedom: in the wild, the tiger is magnificent, a king of the jungle; in the zoo, he is reduced to an object of curiosity. The lesson is that we must respect the natural world and recognise that animals are not possessions but fellow beings with needs, instincts and feelings. Zoos, as the poem suggests, serve human curiosity, not animal welfare — and our relationship with wild creatures should be one of respect, not captivity.

entries.prompt: How does the poet create sympathy for the tiger?
entries.answer: The poet creates sympathy through perspective, imagery and emotion. By entering the tiger's mind — imagining what he should be doing in the wild — the poet makes the reader feel the tiger's loss from the inside. The images of the caged tiger (pacing on velvet-soft pads, staring at the stars, hiding his quiet rage) evoke pity, while the images of the wild tiger (lurking, snarling, terrorising) evoke admiration, making the contrast heartbreaking. The circular structure — ending with the tiger still in his cage, watched by patrolling cars — leaves the reader with a sense of sadness and helplessness. The poet's gentle, precise language and his description of the tiger's suppressed anger make the reader feel the injustice of captivity as keenly as the tiger feels it.

entries.prompt: Why does the poet describe the tiger's eyes as "brilliant"?
entries.answer: The poet describes the tiger's eyes as "brilliant" to emphasise his natural magnificence and to contrast it with the darkness of his cage. The word suggests brightness, power and life — qualities that make the tiger a magnificent creature in the wild. But in the cage, this brilliance is wasted: the tiger stares at the brilliant stars he can never reach, and the light in his eyes is not seen by anyone except curious visitors whom he ignores. The repetition of "brilliant" highlights the tragedy: a creature of such brilliance, confined to a few steps of darkness. The word also connects the tiger to the stars — both are brilliant, but only the stars are free.

entries.prompt: How does the poem's structure reflect its theme of captivity?
entries.answer: The poem's structure mirrors its theme of captivity. It begins in the cage, moves into the wild imagination, and returns to the cage at the end — a circular structure that suggests the tiger can never escape. Just as the tiger is trapped within his cage, the poem itself returns to the same bars; the imaginative flight to the jungle is only a dream that ends in the reality of confinement. The regular four-line stanzas and controlled rhyme scheme also create a sense of order and enclosure, reflecting the disciplined, artificial world of the zoo. Even the language tightens at the end — the final stanza is shorter and more clipped — as if the poem itself is pacing behind bars. The structure thus reinforces the theme: captivity is inescapable, and freedom exists only in imagination.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — Tricki's overindulgent owner
entries.answer: The story is narrated by James Herriot, a veterinary surgeon. Mrs Pumphrey, a rich and doting lady, brings her pet dog Tricki to him. Tricki is a small Pekinese who has become enormously fat. Mrs Pumphrey explains that she feeds him cod-liver oil and malt, sometimes two eggs at a time, and a bowl of Horlicks at eleven o'clock, along with other rich foods. Herriot warns her that this overfeeding is dangerous and that Tricki must be put on a strict diet, but Mrs Pumphrey cannot bear to see her darling hungry. She continues to overfeed the dog, and Tricki's condition worsens: he becomes lazy, listless and refuses to eat, and eventually Mrs Pumphrey, alarmed, brings him to Herriot's surgery.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The "hospital" treatment
entries.answer: When Tricki arrives at the surgery, he is in a sorry state — bloated, lethargic and barely moving. Herriot realises that the cure is not medicine but discipline: the dog needs to be starved and exercised. He decides to keep Tricki at the surgery for a fortnight. He tells Mrs Pumphrey that Tricki must be hospitalised, and although she is reluctant, she agrees. At the surgery, Tricki is put in a kennel with other dogs, and he is given no rich food — only a plain diet. At first, Tricki refuses to eat, but after a day he begins to recover, and soon he is joining the other dogs in their meals and their play.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The recovery
entries.answer: Tricki makes a remarkable recovery. The plain food, the exercise and the company of the other dogs work wonders: he becomes active, playful and hungry. He joins the other dogs in their morning exercises and eats heartily. When Mrs Pumphrey visits, she is amazed at the change in her pet. Herriot, however, decides to keep Tricki a little longer, because the dog is doing so well. Mrs Pumphrey's daily visits bring gifts — initially meals and then, as she grows more anxious, junk foods and delicacies — which the narrator and his partners enjoy themselves, saving the best for Tricki.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The triumphant return
entries.answer: When Tricki is finally discharged, he is transformed: lean, active and full of life. Mrs Pumphrey is overjoyed at the "triumph of surgery" and showers the narrator with gratitude. As the car drives away, Tricki is happy and alert, and Herriot reflects on the real secret of the cure: it was not surgery or medicine but simple common sense — a strict diet and exercise. The title is ironic: the "triumph" was not of surgery but of good veterinary judgement, and of the discipline that the doting Mrs Pumphrey could never enforce herself.

entries.prompt: The dangers of overindulgence
entries.answer: The central theme is the danger of overindulgence. Mrs Pumphrey's excessive love for Tricki — feeding him rich food, eggs and Horlicks — nearly kills him. The story shows that too much of a good thing is harmful: love must be balanced with discipline, and animals (like children) need a healthy diet and exercise. The theme warns against spoiling, showing that true care sometimes means saying no.

entries.prompt: Common sense and professional judgement
entries.answer: The story celebrates common sense and professional judgement. Herriot knows that Tricki does not need medicine but discipline — the "treatment" is a plain diet and exercise. He also handles Mrs Pumphrey with tact, pretending to "hospitalise" the dog to protect her feelings while actually applying simple veterinary sense. The theme shows that expertise lies not in complex solutions but in understanding the real problem and treating it with practical wisdom.

entries.prompt: Mrs Pumphrey
entries.answer: Mrs Pumphrey is a rich, doting and comically overprotective dog owner. She is convinced that her love for Tricki is expressed through food — cod-liver oil, malt, eggs and Horlicks — and she cannot bear to see him hungry. Her visits to the surgery bring a flood of delicacies, which she assumes the "poor dear" needs. Yet her love is sincere, and her joy at Tricki's recovery is genuine. She represents well-meaning but misguided affection, and her name itself — "Pumphrey", pompous-sounding — hints at her comic excess.

entries.prompt: Tricki
entries.answer: Tricki is the spoilt Pekinese at the centre of the story. He is enormously fat, lazy and listless because of his owner's overfeeding. At the surgery, he revives on a plain diet and exercise, becoming playful and healthy. His transformation is the "triumph" of the title — though the triumph belongs to the common sense of the vet, not to surgery. Tricki represents the victim of excessive love: an animal harmed by kindness without discipline.

entries.prompt: Dr James Herriot (the narrator)
entries.answer: Herriot is a wise, observant and good-humoured veterinary surgeon. He diagnoses Tricki's real problem instantly — not illness but overfeeding — and prescribes the simplest cure: diet and exercise. He is also a skilled diplomat: he knows how to handle Mrs Pumphrey, using the word "hospital" to satisfy her while actually applying plain common sense. His humour is gentle, and his joy at Tricki's recovery, and at the delicacies Mrs Pumphrey sends, shows his warm, down-to-earth character. He embodies the professional who looks past the surface to the real problem.

entries.prompt: Discipline and balance in caring
entries.answer: The story teaches that true care requires balance and discipline. Mrs Pumphrey's love was all indulgence and no limits, and it nearly killed Tricki. The lesson is that whether caring for animals, children or ourselves, we must combine affection with healthy habits — moderation, exercise and sensible limits are forms of love too.

entries.prompt: Trust in professional expertise
entries.answer: The story shows the value of trusting professional judgement. Mrs Pumphrey, alarmed by Tricki's condition, follows Herriot's advice, and her trust saves her pet. Herriot's treatment — simple, sensible, non-medical — proves that expertise is not about complicated remedies but about understanding the true cause of a problem.

entries.prompt: Who was Tricki and what was his problem?
entries.answer: Tricki was Mrs Pumphrey's small Pekinese dog. His problem was obesity: he had become enormously fat and listless because his owner overfed him with rich foods, eggs and Horlicks.

entries.prompt: What did Mrs Pumphrey feed Tricki?
entries.answer: She fed him cod-liver oil and malt, sometimes two eggs at a time, a bowl of Horlicks at eleven o'clock, and other rich foods.

entries.prompt: What was Herriot's real treatment for Tricki?
entries.answer: Herriot's real treatment was not medicine but discipline: he put Tricki on a plain diet, kept him in a kennel with other dogs and let him exercise and play.

entries.prompt: Why did Tricki's condition worsen at home?
entries.answer: Despite Herriot's warning, Mrs Pumphrey could not stop overfeeding Tricki, and the rich food made him lazier, more bloated and listless, until he refused to eat and could barely move.

entries.prompt: How did Tricki recover at the surgery?
entries.answer: At the surgery, Tricki was starved of rich food and given a plain diet; he joined the other dogs in their meals and exercises, and his health returned within a few days.

entries.prompt: What did Mrs Pumphrey bring on her visits to the surgery?
entries.answer: She brought gifts — initially meals and then, growing anxious, junk foods and delicacies such as cream cakes and chocolates, which the narrator and his partners enjoyed.

entries.prompt: Why is the title "A Triumph of Surgery" ironic?
entries.answer: The title is ironic because no surgery was performed — Tricki was cured by plain diet and exercise, the common sense of the vet, not by any surgical operation.

entries.prompt: How did Tricki look when he was discharged?
entries.answer: Tricki was transformed: lean, active and full of life, his coat glossy, completely changed from the bloated, listless dog that had arrived.

entries.prompt: How did Mrs Pumphrey's love for Tricki nearly kill him?
entries.answer: Mrs Pumphrey's love for Tricki was expressed entirely through food. She fed him cod-liver oil and malt, two eggs at a time, a bowl of Horlicks at eleven o'clock and other rich foods, unable to bear the thought of him being hungry. Herriot warned her that Tricki must be put on a strict diet, but she could not follow the advice — her love was all indulgence and no discipline. The overfeeding made Tricki enormously fat, lazy and listless; his condition worsened until he refused to eat and could barely move. Her kindness, in short, was killing him: he needed hunger and exercise, and she gave him abundance and comfort. The story shows how love without wisdom can harm the very being it seeks to protect.

entries.prompt: Describe the treatment Herriot gave Tricki at the surgery.
entries.answer: Herriot's treatment was a masterclass in simplicity. He kept Tricki at the surgery for a fortnight, putting him in a kennel with other dogs. The first day, Tricki was listless and refused to eat. But Herriot let hunger do its work: with no rich food available, the dog began to eat the plain meals given to all the dogs, and soon he was joining them in their morning exercises and play. The plain diet, the company of other dogs and the exercise worked wonders — Tricki became active, hungry and healthy. When Mrs Pumphrey visited, she was amazed at the change. Herriot kept the dog a little longer because he was doing so well. The treatment reveals Herriot's insight: the cure was not medicine but the restoration of natural habits — food in moderation and exercise.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about the true meaning of care?
entries.answer: The story teaches that true care is not the same as indulgence. Mrs Pumphrey loved Tricki dearly, but her love took the form of excessive feeding that nearly killed him. Herriot, who cared for the dog professionally, understood that real care meant discipline: a plain diet, exercise and sensible limits. The lesson is that caring for someone — an animal, a child or ourselves — requires balance and wisdom. We must say no sometimes, impose healthy habits and resist the temptation to give in to every want. The story also teaches us to trust experts: Mrs Pumphrey's trust in Herriot saved her pet. And it teaches a touch of humility: the "triumph of surgery" was really a triumph of common sense, reminding us that the simplest solutions are often the most effective.

entries.prompt: Why is the story humorous? Give examples.
entries.answer: The story is humorous because of its characters and situations. Mrs Pumphrey is a comic figure: her "sincere" belief that Tricki needs cod-liver oil, eggs and Horlicks, and her horror at the idea of him going hungry, are absurdly overprotective. Her daily visits, growing more desperate, bring a flood of junk food — cream cakes, chocolates and delicacies — which the narrator and his partners enjoy while pretending they are for Tricki. The narrator's dry humour ("the supply of junk food was cut off by a sudden change in his condition") and his candid admission that the household lived on the offerings add to the comedy. Tricki himself — a fat, lazy dog who revives on a plain diet — is comic, and the final irony — the "triumph of surgery" being no surgery at all — gives the story its smiling punchline.

entries.prompt: How does Herriot handle Mrs Pumphrey? What does this reveal about his character?
entries.answer: Herriot handles Mrs Pumphrey with tact, humour and gentle authority. He knows that telling her directly to starve her beloved dog would cause an uproar, so he frames the treatment as "hospitalisation" — a word that appeals to her anxious care. He allows her visits and accepts her gifts without complaint, maintaining a professional patience with her comic excess. His decision to keep Tricki longer than needed, because the dog is thriving, shows his practical wisdom. These details reveal Herriot's character: he is kind (he never humiliates Mrs Pumphrey), wise (he treats the real problem, not the symptoms), patient (he endures her visits and gifts) and good-humoured (he enjoys the irony of the situation). He is the model of the caring professional who combines expertise with humanity.

entries.prompt: What lesson does the story give about the relationship between owners and their pets?
entries.answer: The story teaches that the relationship between owners and pets should be based on the pet's needs, not the owner's emotions. Mrs Pumphrey loved Tricki, but she treated him as a child to be indulged rather than a dog to be cared for, and her emotional feeding nearly killed him. The lesson is that pets are living beings with natural needs — a healthy diet, exercise and discipline — and that responsible ownership means providing those needs even when it is hard. It also teaches that owners should listen to professionals: Herriot's advice was sound, and following it saved Tricki. Finally, the story suggests that a pet's happiness lies in health and activity, not in pampering — Tricki was never happier than when he was running and eating plain food with the other dogs.

entries.prompt: Stanza-wise meaning
entries.answer: The poem alternates between the voice of an adult (probably a parent) nagging Amanda, and Amanda's own daydreaming. The adult tells Amanda not to bite her nails, not to hunch her shoulders, to stop slouching and to sit up straight — a stream of constant instructions and corrections. In between, Amanda escapes into her imagination: she dreams of being a mermaid drifting blissfully in a languid, emerald sea; of being an orphan wandering freely over the sea's edge; of being Rapunzel, living a tranquil life in a tower, though she quickly realises that even Rapunzel was bothered by someone (the prince) climbing her hair. The poem ends with the adult asking Amanda if she has finished her homework, whether the readers of her poems have arrived, and warning her not to eat chocolate — to which Amanda quietly says she hopes they've all been driven away by "the man" so she can be free.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves in a pattern of nagging and escape. Each stanza of parental instruction is followed by a stanza of Amanda's fantasy: the mermaid, the orphan, Rapunzel. The adult's voice grows sharper and more demanding — from corrections about posture and nails to questions about homework and warnings about chocolate — while Amanda's dreams grow more elaborate and more clearly a retreat from her real life. The poem's movement thus dramatises the tension between the constant demands of adults and the inner freedom of a child's imagination. The ending is poignant: Amanda's final dream is of being left alone, and her final spoken wish is that "the man" (the prince of the Rapunzel story) is gone, so that she can live undisturbed — a child's plea for peace and freedom.

entries.prompt: The tyranny of constant nagging
entries.answer: The central theme is the pressure of constant parental nagging on a child. The adult's stream of instructions — don't bite your nails, don't hunch your shoulders, sit up straight, finish your homework, don't eat chocolate — never stops, and it never acknowledges Amanda's feelings. The poem shows how such relentless correction can suffocate a child, making her retreat into a dream world. The theme criticises parenting that controls instead of communicates.

entries.prompt: The freedom of imagination
entries.answer: The poem celebrates the child's imagination as a refuge. Amanda escapes her nagging world by dreaming: she is a mermaid, an orphan, Rapunzel — figures of freedom and solitude. The poem shows that imagination is not laziness but a vital inner space where a child can be herself. The theme suggests that children need freedom, solitude and space to dream, and that imagination is a healthy response to an over-controlled life.

entries.prompt: Amanda
entries.answer: Amanda is a young girl caught between adult demands and her own dreams. On the surface, she is quiet and obedient — she does not argue with the nagging, but silently escapes into fantasy. Her dreams reveal her true self: she yearns for freedom (the mermaid), for solitude (the orphan), and for a peaceful life without interference (Rapunzel). Her final words — hoping the prince is gone so she can be alone — show her deepest wish: to be left in peace. Amanda is a sensitive child whose imagination is her defence against a world that never stops correcting her.

entries.prompt: The adult (parent)
entries.answer: The adult is an unseen presence whose voice fills the poem with instructions and questions. Though the adult is never described, the voice is clearly parental: it corrects Amanda's posture and habits, demands her homework be done, and warns her against chocolate. The adult is not cruel but unseeing — so busy correcting Amanda that she never sees the child's inner world. The adult represents the well-meaning but overbearing parenting that can stifle a child's spirit.

entries.prompt: Structure and rhyme
entries.answer: The poem alternates between stanzas of the adult's voice and stanzas of Amanda's dreams, creating a pattern of nagging and escape. The rhyme scheme is regular (aaba ccc), giving the poem a musical, almost nursery-verse quality. The parenthetical stanzas containing Amanda's dreams are set off by brackets, visually separating her inner world from the outer world of instruction. The structure itself dramatises the poem's theme: Amanda's dreams are literally enclosed, like her, by the adult's demands.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone of the adult's voice is impatient, repetitive and controlling — a constant stream of commands. The tone of Amanda's sections is dreamy, wistful and longing. The contrast between the two voices creates the poem's mood: at first light and humorous, gradually becoming more poignant as we realise how trapped Amanda feels. The final stanza, with Amanda's quiet hope for solitude, turns the humour into pathos — the poem ends with a child's gentle plea for freedom.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem's imagery is drawn from Amanda's dreams: the languid, emerald sea, the blissful mermaid, the sea's edge where the orphan wanders, the tranquil tower of Rapunzel. Each image symbolises a different form of freedom: the sea symbolises blissful drifting without demands; the orphan's life symbolises solitude and self-determination; the tower symbolises peace — though Amanda recognises even Rapunzel was "haunted" by the prince climbing her hair, showing that no freedom is complete. The imagery reveals Amanda's inner world and her longing for a life without control.

entries.prompt: ALLUSION
entries.answer: The poem alludes to the fairy tale of Rapunzel and to mermaids and orphans — figures of folklore and story. Amanda's wish to be Rapunzel shows her desire for a tranquil life, but she immediately notes that even Rapunzel had her prince climbing her hair, an allusion that reveals the impossibility of perfect solitude.

entries.prompt: ANAPHORA
entries.answer: The adult's commands begin with the repeated word "Don't" ("Don't bite your nails, Amanda!", "Don't hunch your shoulders", "Don't eat that chocolate"), creating a barrage of prohibitions. The anaphora makes the nagging feel relentless and inescapable.

entries.prompt: REPETITION
entries.answer: The name "Amanda" is repeated at the end of almost every command, like a hammer of attention: "Amanda!", "Amanda!". The repetition shows how constantly the child is called and corrected — she can never be free of the adult's voice, which keeps summoning her back.

entries.prompt: PARENTHESIS (BRACKETS)
entries.answer: Amanda's dreams are enclosed in parentheses within the poem, visually separating her inner world from the adult's voice. The brackets are a structural device that dramatises the theme: Amanda's imagination is a private, enclosed space, set apart from the outer world of demands.

entries.prompt: CONTRAST
entries.answer: The poem is built on the contrast between the adult's sharp commands and Amanda's dreamy escapes; between the real world (nails, shoulders, homework, chocolate) and the fantasy world (mermaid, orphan, Rapunzel); between control and freedom. The contrasts make the child's longing vivid.

entries.prompt: IMAGERY
entries.answer: Amanda's dreams create powerful images: a mermaid drifting in a languid, emerald sea, an orphan wandering by the sea's edge, Rapunzel in her tranquil tower. The imagery is soft, liquid and free, contrasting with the sharp, repetitive commands of the adult, and it reveals the child's inner longing for peace.

entries.prompt: RHYME SCHEME (AABA CCC)
entries.answer: The poem follows a regular rhyme scheme, with the adult's quatrains rhyming aaba and Amanda's tercets rhyming ccc. The musicality gives the poem a deceptively light, nursery-verse quality that contrasts with the poem's poignant theme.

entries.prompt: What are the instructions given to Amanda by the adult?
entries.answer: The adult tells Amanda not to bite her nails, not to hunch her shoulders, to stop slouching, to sit up straight, to finish her homework, and not to eat chocolate.

entries.prompt: What does Amanda dream of being in the poem?
entries.answer: Amanda dreams of being a mermaid drifting blissfully in a languid, emerald sea, an orphan wandering freely by the sea's edge, and Rapunzel living in a tranquil tower.

entries.prompt: Why does Amanda think even Rapunzel's life was not perfect?
entries.answer: Amanda realises that even Rapunzel was disturbed — the prince kept climbing up her hair. So she hopes the prince (whom she calls "the man") has been driven away, leaving her in peace.

entries.prompt: How does the poet visually separate Amanda's dreams from the adult's voice?
entries.answer: Amanda's dreams are written in parentheses (brackets) within the poem, while the adult's commands are written in the main text — a visual separation of her inner world from the outer world of demands.

entries.prompt: What does the mermaid symbolise in Amanda's dream?
entries.answer: The mermaid drifting in a languid, emerald sea symbolises Amanda's longing for freedom and bliss — a life without demands, gliding peacefully through a beautiful, serene world.

entries.prompt: What is the effect of the repetition of "Amanda!"?
entries.answer: The repetition of "Amanda!" at the end of the adult's commands shows how constantly the child is called and corrected. It makes the nagging feel relentless and inescapable.

entries.prompt: What is the rhyme scheme of the poem?
entries.answer: The poem follows a regular pattern — aaba for the adult's quatrains and ccc for Amanda's tercets — giving it a musical, nursery-verse quality.

entries.prompt: What is the central theme of the poem?
entries.answer: The central theme is the pressure of constant nagging on a child and the importance of freedom and imagination. Amanda escapes her over-controlled life through dreams of freedom and solitude.

entries.prompt: How does the poet present the conflict between the adult and the child in "Amanda!"?
entries.answer: The poet presents the conflict through alternating voices. The adult's voice is a relentless stream of commands and questions: don't bite your nails, don't hunch your shoulders, stop slouching, sit up straight, finish your homework, don't eat chocolate. Amanda's response is silence — she never argues — but her dreams speak for her: in her imagination she is a mermaid, an orphan, Rapunzel, figures of freedom and solitude. The conflict is between control and freedom: the adult wants to shape Amanda into a proper child, while Amanda wants only to be left alone. The brackets around her dreams visually dramatise the conflict — her inner world is enclosed, private, separate from the world of demands. The poem suggests that such constant correction, however well-meaning, suffocates a child's spirit, and that children need space to dream.

entries.prompt: What do Amanda's dreams reveal about her character?
entries.answer: Amanda's dreams reveal a sensitive, imaginative child who longs for freedom, solitude and peace. As a mermaid drifting in a languid, emerald sea, she yearns for a life of blissful freedom, without demands or correction. As an orphan wandering by the sea's edge, she imagines solitude as liberation — a life where no one tells her what to do. As Rapunzel, she dreams of a tranquil life in a tower, but she immediately recognises that even Rapunzel was not left in peace, because the prince climbed her hair. This realisation shows Amanda's growing awareness that complete freedom may be impossible — and her final hope that "the man" has been driven away shows her deepest wish: to be undisturbed. Her dreams reveal a child who is not lazy or disobedient but quietly yearning for the space to be herself.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about how children should be treated?
entries.answer: The poem teaches us that children need freedom, respect and space, not constant correction. The adult in the poem is not cruel, but the endless stream of instructions — about nails, posture, homework and chocolate — never once acknowledges Amanda's feelings or inner world. Amanda's retreat into fantasy shows the cost of such treatment: a child who cannot be herself in the real world escapes into imagination. The lesson is that discipline should be balanced with understanding: children should be guided, not controlled; listened to, not only lectured. Parents and teachers should create space for a child's imagination, allow her to make small choices, and show interest in her thoughts and dreams. A child who is heard grows up confident; a child who is only nagged grows up withdrawn. The poem is a gentle reminder to treat children as people, not projects.

entries.prompt: Why does Amanda wish to be an orphan in her dream?
entries.answer: Amanda's wish to be an orphan is striking because it seems so tragic, yet to her it represents freedom. An orphan, in her imagination, has no one to nag her, no one to correct her posture, no one to demand homework — she can wander freely by the sea's edge, alone and unobserved. The wish reveals how suffocated Amanda feels by the adult's constant attention: even the tragic fate of being parentless appears to her as liberation. This is the poem's poignant irony — a child would rather imagine herself alone in the world than live one more day under the relentless voice of correction. The dream shows that what Amanda needs is not more instruction but solitude and space, and that her imagination, however sad its images, is her way of claiming freedom in a world that gives her none.

entries.prompt: How does the ending of the poem reinforce its theme?
entries.answer: The ending of the poem reinforces its theme of a child's longing for freedom. The adult's final questions — about homework, about the readers of her poems — are followed by a final warning not to eat chocolate. Amanda's quiet reply is a wish: she hopes the readers and the "man" (the prince from her Rapunzel dream) have all been driven away, so that she can finally be free. The ending shows that Amanda's dream life is not just play but a deep need: her greatest hope is to be left alone, unobserved and unbothered. The adult, meanwhile, remains unaware of Amanda's inner world, still busy with corrections and warnings. The poem thus ends in pathos: the nagging continues, and Amanda's only escape remains her imagination. The theme — that constant control suffocates children and that freedom is their deepest need — is quietly driven home.

entries.prompt: Comment on the significance of the title "Amanda!".
entries.answer: The title "Amanda!" — with its exclamation mark — captures the tone of the adult's voice throughout the poem. It is a summons, a correction, a command: the child's name is called again and again, always with an instruction attached. The title thus represents the constant attention under which Amanda lives — she can never simply be; she is always being told to be something else. The exclamation mark is the adult's impatience made visible. Yet the title also carries the poem's irony: for all the calling of her name, the adult never really sees Amanda — her dreams, her longings, her need for freedom. The title, like the poem, is about a child who is named, nagged and never understood. It is a call that is answered only in silence, and in dreams.

entries.prompt: Stanza-wise meaning
entries.answer: In the first stanza, the poet declares that he could turn and live with animals — they are so placid and self-contained. He says that he stands and looks at them for a long time, and they do not make him feel uneasy or ashamed. In the second stanza, the poet lists the qualities of animals that he admires: they do not sweat and whine about their condition, they do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, they do not make him sick discussing their duty to God, and not one of them is dissatisfied or demented with the mania of owning things. In the third stanza, the poet says that animals do not show respect to him or to each other — not one is humble or demented with the mania of owning things, and they show their relations to him and to each other without any pretence. Finally, the poet wonders whether he had passed the way of animals "huge times ago" and negligently dropped his tokens of selfhood — and he says that animals do not stay awake for hours talking about their duty to God, nor are they demented with the mania of owning things.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves from admiration to criticism. The poet begins by declaring his wish to live with animals, praising their placid, self-contained nature. He then contrasts the animals with humans, listing the vices of humanity: complaining, guilt, religious hypocrisy, dissatisfaction and greed. The animals, he says, possess what humans have lost: contentment, simplicity and honest relations. The poem ends with a poignant question: did the poet himself once possess these virtues and "negligently" drop them in his journey through life? The movement of the poem is thus from the present (the poet looking at animals) to the past (the poet wondering about his lost selfhood), and from admiration of animals to self-criticism of humanity.

entries.prompt: The superiority of animal simplicity over human complexity
entries.answer: The central theme is the contrast between the simplicity of animals and the complexity, greed and hypocrisy of humans. Animals are placid, self-contained and content; humans are dissatisfied, guilt-ridden and obsessed with possessions. The poem suggests that in our rush to "improve" ourselves — through religion, money and status — we have lost the very virtues that make life peaceful, and that animals, in their simplicity, retain what we have lost.

entries.prompt: Criticism of materialism and hypocrisy
entries.answer: The poem is a sharp critique of human materialism and hypocrisy. The poet criticises humans for their "mania of owning things", their dissatisfaction with their condition, their weeping over sins and their empty talk of duty to God. The animals, who own nothing and pretend nothing, are shown as morally superior. The theme satirises the values of modern society, where greed and show are prized above contentment and truth.

entries.prompt: The poet/speaker
entries.answer: The speaker is a reflective, self-critical observer who longs for a simpler life. He admires animals for their placid contentment and honesty, and he is ashamed of humanity — and, perhaps, of himself. His question at the end — whether he once possessed the virtues of animals and carelessly lost them — reveals his longing to recover that lost simplicity. The speaker is Whitman himself, a poet famous for celebrating nature, simplicity and the dignity of the common life.

entries.prompt: The animals
entries.answer: The animals of the poem are idealised figures: placid, self-contained and content. They do not complain about their condition, do not weep over sins, do not discuss duty to God, do not own anything and do not pretend. They show their relations to one another and to the poet without any pretence. The animals are not described individually but as a collective ideal — the embodiment of the simplicity and honesty that humans have lost.

entries.prompt: Structure and form
entries.answer: The poem is written in free verse — it has no regular rhyme scheme or metre. Whitman's free verse is famous for its natural, flowing rhythm, which suits his theme: like the animals he describes, the poem is unadorned and honest. The long, flowing lines and the repetition of key phrases give the poem a meditative, chant-like quality. The form reflects the poem's message — simplicity and naturalness over artifice and ornament.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone of the poem is reflective, admiring and gently critical. The poet's admiration for animals is genuine and tender, while his criticism of humanity is sharp but not bitter — it carries a note of longing rather than anger. The mood is contemplative: the poet stands and looks at animals for a long time, and the poem's slow, flowing rhythm invites the reader to pause and reflect with him. The ending, with its question about lost selfhood, adds a touch of wistfulness and regret.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem's imagery is drawn from everyday life: animals standing placid and self-contained, humans sweating and whining, lying awake weeping, discussing duty to God, and being demented with the mania of owning things. The animals symbolise simplicity, contentment and honesty — the virtues humans have lost. Human traits — dissatisfaction, greed, hypocrisy — are symbolised by the vices the poet lists. The poem's imagery is not visual but moral: it paints a picture of two ways of living, and asks the reader to choose.

entries.prompt: ANAPHORA
entries.answer: The poem uses anaphora heavily: "They do not sweat and whine...", "They do not lie awake...", "They do not make me sick...", "Not one is dissatisfied...". The repetition of "They do not" creates a rhythmic list of human vices and animal virtues, making the contrast emphatic and memorable.

entries.prompt: REPETITION
entries.answer: Key phrases are repeated for emphasis: "so placid and self-contained", "not one is dissatisfied", "not one is demented with the mania of owning things". The repetitions hammer home the poem's message — the animals' contentment and freedom from greed — and give the free verse its chant-like rhythm.

entries.prompt: PERSONIFICATION (IN REVERSE)
entries.answer: The poet attributes human qualities to animals in order to criticise humans: animals "do not sweat and whine about their condition" and "do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins" — traits that humans possess. By describing animals in human terms, the poet measures human behaviour against animal simplicity and finds humanity wanting.

entries.prompt: METAPHOR
entries.answer: The "mania of owning things" is a metaphor for the human obsession with possessions and wealth — described as a kind of madness. The metaphor is vivid and damning: greed is not a normal human trait but a mania, a mental disease that animals are mercifully free from.

entries.prompt: RHETORICAL QUESTION
entries.answer: The poem ends with a rhetorical question: "Did I pass that way huge times ago and negligently drop my tokens of selfhood?" The question is not asked for information but for reflection — it suggests that the poet (and humanity) once possessed the virtues of animals and carelessly lost them, and it invites the reader to ask the same question of themselves.

entries.prompt: ALLITERATION
entries.answer: The poem uses alliteration for musical effect, as in "so placid and self-contained", "sweat and whine", and "long and long". The repeated consonant sounds give the free verse a subtle rhythm and bind the phrases together.

entries.prompt: HYPERBOLE
entries.answer: The poet exaggerates human faults to make his point: humans lie awake "in the dark" weeping for their sins, make him "sick" discussing duty to God, and are "demented" with the mania of owning things. The hyperbole sharpens the satire against human hypocrisy and greed.

entries.prompt: What does the poet wish to do in the poem?
entries.answer: The poet wishes to "turn and live with animals" — to leave the complex, greedy world of humans and live among animals, which are placid and self-contained.

entries.prompt: Why do animals not make the poet feel uneasy?
entries.answer: The animals do not make the poet feel uneasy because they are honest and unpretentious — they do not complain, pretend or show off, and they accept the poet without judgment.

entries.prompt: What do animals not do, according to the poet?
entries.answer: Animals do not sweat and whine about their condition, do not lie awake weeping for their sins, do not discuss duty to God, are not dissatisfied, and are not demented with the mania of owning things.

entries.prompt: What is the "mania of owning things"?
entries.answer: The "mania of owning things" is the human obsession with possessions and wealth — a greed that the poet describes as a kind of madness, from which animals are free.

entries.prompt: How do animals show their relations to the poet?
entries.answer: Animals show their relations to the poet and to each other "without any pretence" — openly and honestly, without the hypocrisy and show that mark human relationships.

entries.prompt: What does the poet mean by "tokens of selfhood"?
entries.answer: "Tokens of selfhood" are the marks of one's true self — the virtues like simplicity, contentment and honesty. The poet wonders whether he once possessed these and negligently dropped them on his journey through life.

entries.prompt: What is the form of the poem?
entries.answer: The poem is written in free verse — no regular rhyme scheme or metre — reflecting Whitman's natural, flowing style and the poem's theme of simplicity.

entries.prompt: What does the poet criticise in human beings?
entries.answer: The poet criticises human dissatisfaction, guilt, religious hypocrisy and greed — the vices that animals, in their simplicity, do not possess.

entries.prompt: What are the qualities of animals that the poet admires?
entries.answer: The poet admires animals for their placid, self-contained nature. They are content with their condition and do not complain or "sweat and whine" about their lot in life. They do not suffer from guilt, lying awake in the dark weeping for their sins. They are free of religious hypocrisy — they do not discuss their duty to God as humans do.
