They are not dissatisfied, and they are not obsessed with possessions, being free from the "mania of owning things". Finally, they are honest: they show their relations to the poet and to each other without any pretence. In short, the poet admires animals for the virtues humans have lost — contentment, simplicity, honesty and freedom from greed and hypocrisy.

entries.prompt: How does the poet contrast animals with human beings?
entries.answer: The poet builds the poem on a sustained contrast between animals and humans. Animals are placid and self-contained; humans are restless and dissatisfied. Animals accept their condition; humans "sweat and whine" about theirs. Animals are free of guilt; humans "lie awake in the dark" weeping for their sins. Animals do not discuss duty to God; humans talk about it endlessly, and the poet says such talk makes him "sick". Animals own nothing and are content; humans are "demented with the mania of owning things". Animals relate honestly, without pretence; humans are full of show and hypocrisy. The contrast is one-sided: the animals come out morally superior on every count, and the poem implies that in our progress as civilised beings, we have lost the simplicity and integrity that would make us truly happy.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about the way we live?
entries.answer: The poem teaches us to question the values of modern life. We rush to own more, to appear better, to discuss virtue — yet the poet shows that these very activities make us dissatisfied, guilty and hypocritical. The animals, who own nothing and pretend nothing, are content. The lesson is that happiness lies in simplicity: accepting our condition, being honest in our relations, and freeing ourselves from the "mania of owning things". The poem also teaches us to reflect on ourselves — the poet's question about his dropped "tokens of selfhood" invites us to ask whether we, too, have lost our true selves in the pursuit of wealth and status. Contentment, honesty and peace are within our reach if we simplify our lives and learn from the natural world around us.

entries.prompt: What is the significance of the poet's question at the end of the poem?
entries.answer: The poet's final question — "Did I pass that way huge times ago and negligently drop my tokens of selfhood?" — is the poem's emotional climax. It suggests that the virtues of the animals are not foreign to humanity but were once our own: the poet imagines that, long ago, human beings passed through the same stage of life as the animals and possessed the same simplicity, contentment and honesty. But in the journey of civilisation, we "negligently" — carelessly, without noticing — dropped these tokens of our true selfhood, trading them for greed, hypocrisy and dissatisfaction. The question transforms the poem from a criticism of humans into a lament: we did not lose our virtues through any evil but through neglect. The question also invites the reader to self-reflection — have we, too, dropped our true selves somewhere along the way, and can we recover them?

entries.prompt: Why does the poet say that animals "do not make him sick discussing their duty to God"?
entries.answer: The poet says animals "do not make me sick discussing their duty to God" to satirise human religious hypocrisy. Humans talk endlessly about their duty to God, using religious language to appear virtuous while often being greedy, unkind and dishonest in their actual lives. The poet is "sick" of this talk because it is empty — it is pretence, not goodness. The animals, by contrast, do not discuss their duty to God at all, yet they live naturally and honestly, without pretence or hypocrisy. The line is a sharp criticism of those who use religion as a show, and it suggests that true virtue lies not in talking about duty but in living simply and truthfully — the way the animals do.

entries.prompt: How does Whitman's free verse contribute to the poem's effect?
entries.answer: Whitman's free verse is essential to the poem's effect. Without the artificial constraints of rhyme and metre, the poem flows naturally, like the spontaneous thoughts of the poet as he stands and looks at the animals. The long, flowing lines and the repetitions ("They do not...", "Not one is...") create a chant-like rhythm that mirrors the poet's meditative state and the placid, steady presence of the animals. The form is also a statement in itself: like the animals, the poem is unadorned and honest, free of the ornaments and tricks of conventional verse. Just as the poet turns away from the pretence of human society, the poem turns away from the pretence of poetic form. Content and form work together: the free verse embodies the simplicity that the poem celebrates.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The neglected child
entries.answer: Bholi, whose real name was Sulekha, was the youngest of Ramlal's seven children. When she was ten months old, she had fallen off the cot and damaged some part of her brain, and her speech became stammering and hesitant. Later, an attack of smallpox left her face permanently scarred with pockmarks. So the family treated her as an ugly, slow girl, and even her real name, Sulekha, was forgotten — everyone called her Bholi, the simpleton. Her parents neglected her, and her sisters, especially her elder sister, treated her with contempt. Bholi grew up feeling inferior and frightened, shunning the company of other children.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The village school
entries.answer: When the village school opened, the tehsildar, during a visit, told Ramlal that he should send his daughters to school. Ramlal was reluctant to send his daughters, but for Bholi — plain and unmarried-able — he decided it would be a way of getting rid of her. So Bholi, for the first time, was dressed in clean clothes and sent to school. She was frightened of the teacher, but the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile made her feel safe. The teacher told her that her name was Sulekha, a beautiful name — and Bholi, hearing it, felt a new respect for herself. That first day, she learnt to say her name without stammering, and the teacher's love began to change her.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The marriage proposal
entries.answer: Years passed, and Bholi grew into a young woman of about fifteen. Ramlal received a marriage proposal from Bishamber Nath, a rich businessman of the neighbouring village, who agreed to marry Bholi because he was attracted by her father's wealth and standing. Ramlal was overjoyed, and the family began preparations. But when the wedding day came, and Bishamber Nath saw Bholi's scarred face, he demanded a dowry of five thousand rupees — and then, even as the wedding ceremony was about to begin, he raised the demand: he would not marry her unless he received the money in cash before the ceremony.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The revolt and the new life
entries.answer: Ramlal, desperate, agreed to give the money, and the marriage continued. But then Bholi spoke — for the first time in her life, clearly and without fear. She refused to marry Bishamber, calling him a "greedy beast" and telling him to keep his money. Everyone was stunned. Bholi declared that she would stay with her parents and look after them, and that she would teach the village children, and that no one could force her to marry against her will. The story ends with Bholi returning home — no longer a frightened, stammering child, but a confident, self-respecting young woman who had, in her own way, become the "cleverest" person in the family.

entries.prompt: The power of education and self-belief
entries.answer: The central theme is the transforming power of education and self-belief. Bholi, neglected and treated as a simpleton, is changed by her teacher's kindness and her years at school. Education gives her not only learning but self-respect: she learns her real name, learns to speak without fear, and finally finds the courage to refuse a greedy groom. The story shows that education, especially of girls, is the greatest weapon against oppression.

entries.prompt: The position of women and the evil of dowry
entries.answer: The story exposes the cruelty of dowry and the low status of women. Bholi is married off for money and her father's prestige; Bishamber demands cash even as the ceremony begins. Bholi's refusal is a revolt against this system. The theme is that a woman is not a commodity to be sold, and that the greed of dowry must be resisted by courage and education.

entries.prompt: Overcoming prejudice and appearances
entries.answer: Bholi is judged by her appearance — her pockmarked face and stammering speech — and treated as worthless by her own family. Her journey shows how cruel such judgments are: the "simpleton" proves the most intelligent and courageous person in the story. The theme is that true worth lies within, and that prejudice based on looks or speech is a blindness the educated heart must cure.

entries.prompt: Bholi (Sulekha)
entries.answer: Bholi is the heroine of the story. Born the youngest of seven children, she is scarred by smallpox and stammers from an early accident, and her family treats her as an ugly simpleton — even forgetting her real name, Sulekha. She grows up shy, frightened and full of self-pity. But two forces change her: the village school, where her teacher's kindness gives her self-respect, and the moment of crisis at her wedding, when she finds her voice and refuses the greedy Bishamber. Her refusal is an act of astonishing courage: she, who could hardly speak, declares that she will not marry a man who demands dowry, and that she will serve her parents and teach the village's children. She is the story's proof that education and self-belief can overcome even the deepest wounds of neglect.

entries.prompt: Bholi's teacher
entries.answer: Bholi's teacher is the quiet heroine behind her transformation. When the frightened, stammering child comes to school, the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile make her feel safe. She tells Bholi that her name, Sulekha, is beautiful, and she teaches her patiently, day after day. Her love gives the child something no one else had given her: respect. The teacher represents the power of the educated woman — the kind, patient guide who shows that the "dullest" child, treated with dignity, can blossom. Bholi's final ambition, to teach village children, is the teacher's gift returned to the world.

entries.prompt: Bishamber Nath
entries.answer: Bishamber Nath is a rich businessman of the neighbouring village, the groom chosen for Bholi. He agrees to the marriage only because of Ramlal's wealth and standing. He is vain, greedy and cruel: when he sees Bholi's scarred face, he insults her by refusing at first, and then agrees on the condition of a heavy dowry — five thousand rupees. Even as the wedding ceremony begins, he raises his demand, insisting on cash before he will proceed. His greed is his undoing: Bholi's refusal shames him publicly, and he slinks away. He represents the selfishness and greed that Bholi's courage must defeat.

entries.prompt: Ramlal
entries.answer: Ramlal is Bholi's father, a numberdar (village official) with seven children. He is a traditional man: he is reluctant to send his daughters to school, and he marries Bholi off for prestige and money. He treats Bholi with indifference, calling her "simpleton", yet he is not evil — he is a victim of the customs of his world, panicking when the marriage is in danger and willing to pay any dowry to save it. His surrender to Bishamber's demands shows the weakness of the old ways; it is his daughter who must teach him courage.

entries.prompt: Girls must be educated
entries.answer: The story is a powerful argument for girls' education. School gives Bholi self-respect, knowledge and the courage to refuse a greedy marriage. The lesson: education liberates — it turns a neglected child into a self-reliant woman, and it is the surest path to equality and dignity.

entries.prompt: Courage to refuse what is wrong
entries.answer: Bholi's refusal of the dowry-seeking groom is a lesson in moral courage. She, who once could not speak, finds the strength to say no to greed and humiliation. The story teaches that standing up for one's dignity — even alone, even against tradition — is a duty, and that self-respect is worth more than wealth.

entries.prompt: What was Bholi's real name?
entries.answer: Her real name was Sulekha, but everyone called her Bholi, meaning "simpleton".

entries.prompt: Why did Bholi stammer?
entries.answer: As a ten-month-old baby, she had fallen off a cot and damaged some part of her brain, which affected her speech.

entries.prompt: What marks did Bholi have on her face?
entries.answer: An attack of smallpox had left her face permanently scarred with pockmarks.

entries.prompt: Why was Bholi sent to school?
entries.answer: When the village school opened, the tehsildar advised Ramlal to send his daughters; for Bholi, plain and unlikely to marry, he saw it as a way of "getting rid of" her.

entries.prompt: How did the teacher change Bholi's life?
entries.answer: Her gentle voice, kind smile and patient teaching gave Bholi self-respect — she learnt her own name, Sulekha, and gained the confidence to speak.

entries.prompt: Who wanted to marry Bholi?
entries.answer: Bishamber Nath, a rich businessman of the neighbouring village, who was attracted by Ramlal's wealth and standing.

entries.prompt: What demand did Bishamber make at the wedding?
entries.answer: He demanded a dowry of five thousand rupees in cash, raising the demand even as the ceremony was about to begin.

entries.prompt: What did Bholi declare at the wedding?
entries.answer: She refused to marry Bishamber, called him a greedy beast, and declared she would serve her parents and teach the village children.

entries.prompt: How did Bholi's family treat her and why?
entries.answer: Bholi was the most neglected child in Ramlal's family. Her stammering speech, caused by a fall as a baby, and the pockmarks left by smallpox made her seem ugly and slow to her parents and sisters. They judged her by her appearance and treated her with indifference and contempt: they forgot her real name and called her Bholi, the simpleton; her elder sisters made her do the household chores while they prepared for their own marriages; and no one thought of her education or future. Her parents even saw her as a burden — when the tehsildar advised sending girls to school, Ramlal agreed only because school would "get rid of" Bholi. The family's neglect filled Bholi with a deep sense of inferiority: she was afraid of people, avoided children and thought herself worthless. The story shows how cruel such neglect is, and how love and respect can heal what it wounds.

entries.prompt: What role did the school and the teacher play in Bholi's transformation?
entries.answer: School and the teacher transformed Bholi's life. On her first day, she was terrified of the classroom, but the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile made her feel safe — "the first time she had ever been called by anyone with affection". The teacher told her that her real name, Sulekha, was a beautiful name, and hearing it with respect gave the child her first taste of self-worth. Day after day, the teacher taught her with patience, and Bholi learnt to speak clearly, to read and write, and to believe in herself. Education gave her more than knowledge: it gave her identity (her name), voice (her speech) and dignity (her sense of worth). By the time of her marriage, the frightened stammering child had become a woman with the courage to refuse a greedy groom. The story's message is clear: education, given with love, can transform even the most neglected child — and that is why the educated woman is the hope of the village.

entries.prompt: Value question: What made Bholi refuse the marriage at the last moment?
entries.answer: Bholi refused the marriage because education had given her self-respect, and self-respect gave her courage. Bishamber Nath's behaviour revealed his true character: he demanded five thousand rupees as dowry, and then raised his demand even as the ceremony began, humiliating Bholi and her family. Bholi remembered her teacher's lessons — that she was a person of worth, not a commodity — and she saw that the man was greedy, not loving. Her refusal was a revolt against dowry, against humiliation and against the idea that a woman must be grateful for any marriage. She declared that she would stay with her parents, look after them and teach the village children, and that no one could force her. Her courage was the fruit of her schooling: the girl who could not speak grew into the woman who would not be bought. Her refusal teaches that dignity is not for sale.

entries.prompt: How does the story criticise the dowry system?
entries.answer: The story is a sharp criticism of the dowry system. Bishamber Nath, a rich man, agrees to marry Bholi only because of her father's wealth; on the wedding day, seeing her scarred face, he at first refuses, and then consents only on condition of a five-thousand-rupee dowry. Even as the ceremony is about to begin, he raises his demand, insisting on cash first — greed and humiliation exposed in full view of the guests. Ramlal, helpless before custom, is ready to pay anything. Bholi's refusal is the story's verdict: a woman is not a business deal, and a marriage based on money is not a marriage at all. By making the heroine of the story — the "simpleton" — the one who rejects the dowry-seeker, the author shows that the evil is not in the victim but in the system, and that courage, born of education, is the only real cure.

entries.prompt: Describe the transformation of Bholi from a child to a young woman.
entries.answer: Bholi's transformation is the heart of the story. As a child, she was the picture of neglect: scarred by smallpox, stammering from an accident, called "simpleton" even by her parents, she was shy, frightened and full of self-pity, shrinking from other children and the world. School began her change: her teacher's kindness gave her the first love she had known, her name Sulekha restored her identity, and her lessons gave her speech, confidence and dreams. As a young woman of fifteen, she was still plain and neglected, but within her grew a quiet strength. The wedding was her crucible: when Bishamber's greed insulted her, she — who once could not utter a sentence — spoke clearly and fearlessly, refused the marriage and declared her own plans for her life. The girl who was considered the family's greatest burden became its greatest pride, and the "simpleton" proved the cleverest of them all.

entries.prompt: Stanza-wise meaning
entries.answer: The poem is a short lyric of eight lines in two stanzas. In the first stanza, the speaker describes a moment when a crow, perched on a hemlock tree, shook down a small amount of snow ("dust of snow") onto him. In the second stanza, the speaker says that this tiny, seemingly insignificant incident changed his mood: it gave his heart "a change of mood" and saved part of a day that he had been regretting. The poem thus captures how a small moment in nature can lift a person out of gloom and transform a day that seemed lost.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves from a negative to a positive state. The speaker begins the day in a sad, regretful mood, and the natural imagery around him — a crow, a hemlock tree, snow — is dark and foreboding. The crow's action of shaking snow onto him could be seen as an annoyance, yet it becomes the turning point of the poem. The falling snow, instead of worsening his mood, refreshes him and brings a change of heart. The poem's movement is thus from despair to relief, showing that nature, even in its darker aspects, has the power to heal. The brevity of the poem mirrors the brevity of the moment it describes: a second of natural wonder that changes a whole day.

entries.prompt: The healing power of nature
entries.answer: The central theme is nature's ability to change our mood and heal our spirit. The speaker is in a state of regret, but the simple falling of snow from a tree revives him. Frost shows that we do not need grand landscapes to be comforted by nature — a crow, a tree and a little snow are enough. The theme suggests that small moments of connection with nature can refresh the mind and save us from despair.

entries.prompt: Small moments, big change
entries.answer: The poem celebrates the idea that great changes can come from small events. A tiny "dust of snow" is a trivial thing, yet it completely transforms the speaker's day. The theme reminds us to stay open to small moments of beauty and grace, because they can arrive unexpectedly and change our perspective on life. It also suggests that we should not undervalue the little things that can lift our spirits.

entries.prompt: The speaker
entries.answer: The speaker begins the poem in a sad and regretful mood, having "rued" his day. He is someone who is sensitive to his own feelings, yet open to the influence of nature: the falling snow instantly changes his mood. His reaction shows a person willing to be touched by small moments of beauty, and the poem records his transformation from gloom to lightness.

entries.prompt: The crow and the hemlock tree
entries.answer: The crow and the hemlock tree are the agents of the speaker's change. In traditional symbolism, crows and hemlocks carry negative associations — the crow is often a bird of ill omen and the hemlock a poisonous plant. Frost deliberately uses these dark images to show that even the most negative elements of nature can bring joy and change of mood. The crow's action is accidental, yet it becomes the instrument of the speaker's healing.

entries.prompt: Structure and rhyme
entries.answer: The poem has a simple structure: two quatrains of four lines each, with a regular rhyme scheme (ABAB CDCD). The simplicity of the form matches the simplicity of the incident described. Frost's use of short, crisp lines gives the poem a light, airy quality that echoes the falling snow, and the poem's brevity reflects the fleeting nature of the moment it captures.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The poem begins in a sombre, regretful tone, with the speaker ruing his day. The mood shifts when the snow falls, becoming lighter, refreshed and almost joyful. The change is swift and subtle, mirroring the suddenness of the natural event. Frost's tone is quiet and reflective, and the poem ends with a sense of quiet gratitude for the small grace that saved the speaker's day.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem is built on vivid natural imagery: the crow, the hemlock tree, the dust of snow. Frost deliberately chooses symbols that are traditionally dark — the crow as a bird of ill omen and the hemlock as a poisonous plant — to prove his point: even negative symbols can bring positive change. The "dust of snow" is itself a symbol of the small, overlooked moments that can transform our mood. The contrast between the darkness of the symbols and the lightness of the outcome creates the poem's depth.

entries.prompt: ALLITERATION
entries.answer: The repetition of consonant sounds: "saved some part", "Has given my heart", "The way a crow". The repeated sounds create a soft, falling rhythm that mimics the gentle fall of snow and binds the lines together musically.

entries.prompt: SYMBOLISM
entries.answer: The crow and the hemlock tree symbolise negative or dark elements, yet they bring about a positive change of mood. The "dust of snow" symbolises the small, seemingly trivial moments of nature that can transform our day. Frost uses this symbolism to show that even darkness can bring light.

entries.prompt: IMAGERY
entries.answer: The poem creates a vivid visual image of a crow shaking snow from a hemlock tree onto the speaker. The imagery is precise and minimal, painting a complete scene in a few strokes. The image of falling snow is cold yet refreshing, and it carries the emotional weight of the poem.

entries.prompt: ENJAMBMENT
entries.answer: Lines run on into the next without punctuation, as in "The way a crow / Shook down on me". The flow of one line into another mirrors the continuous, unbroken fall of snow and the smooth unfolding of the speaker's change of mood.

entries.prompt: UNDERSTATEMENT
entries.answer: The poem describes a profound change of mood through a deliberately small event: "And saved some part / Of a day I had rued." The word "saved" is quiet and modest, yet it carries the weight of the poem's meaning — a whole day, previously ruined, has been rescued by a moment of nature.

entries.prompt: RHYME SCHEME (ABAB CDCD)
entries.answer: The poem follows a regular rhyme scheme, with the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyming ("me"/"tree", "heart"/"part"). The regularity of the rhyme gives the poem a musical, song-like quality that contrasts gently with the seriousness of the speaker's mood, adding to the poem's charm.

entries.prompt: What does the crow do in the poem?
entries.answer: The crow, perched on a hemlock tree, shakes down a small amount of snow ("dust of snow") onto the speaker as he passes beneath.

entries.prompt: What was the speaker's mood before the incident?
entries.answer: The speaker was in a sad, regretful mood — he had "rued" his day, meaning he felt sorry about how his day was going and was in low spirits.

entries.prompt: How did the falling snow change the speaker?
entries.answer: The falling snow gave the speaker's heart "a change of mood". It lifted his gloom and saved part of the day he had been regretting.

entries.prompt: What is the rhyme scheme of the poem?
entries.answer: The rhyme scheme of the poem is ABAB CDCD, with each quatrain following an alternating rhyme pattern.

entries.prompt: Why did Frost choose a crow and a hemlock tree?
entries.answer: Frost deliberately chose the crow and the hemlock tree because both carry dark, negative associations (the crow as an ill-omened bird and the hemlock as a poisonous plant). He wanted to show that even negative elements of nature can bring about positive change.

entries.prompt: What does the "dust of snow" symbolise?
entries.answer: The "dust of snow" symbolises the small, seemingly trivial moments of beauty in nature that can have a profound effect on our mood and transform a day that seemed lost.

entries.prompt: How does the poem's brevity relate to its theme?
entries.answer: The poem's brevity mirrors the brevity of the moment it describes: a single, fleeting second of natural wonder is enough to change a whole day. The short form emphasises that great changes can come from tiny moments.

entries.prompt: What is the central idea of the poem?
entries.answer: The central idea is that nature, even in its smallest and seemingly darkest forms, has the power to change our mood and heal our spirit. A little snow shaken from a tree by a crow can save a day of gloom.

entries.prompt: How does the poem "Dust of Snow" show the healing power of nature?
entries.answer: The poem shows the healing power of nature through a single, small incident. The speaker is in a state of regret and gloom, feeling that his day is ruined. As he walks, a crow shakes a little snow onto him from a hemlock tree. Instead of being annoyed, the speaker finds his mood transformed — the snow gives his heart a "change of mood" and saves part of his day. Frost deliberately uses dark symbols (the crow, the hemlock) to prove that nature's healing does not depend on beautiful scenes: even a dark bird, a poisonous tree and a scrap of snow can lift a heavy heart. The poem suggests that nature is always offering us small gifts of renewal, if we are open to receiving them.

entries.prompt: What is the significance of the crow and the hemlock tree in the poem?
entries.answer: The crow and the hemlock tree are significant because Frost chooses them despite — or because of — their negative associations. A crow is traditionally a bird of ill omen, and the hemlock is a poisonous plant. By placing his healing moment in such a "dark" setting, Frost overturns conventional expectations: the speaker's mood is not lifted by a singing bird in a flowering tree, but by a crow and a hemlock. The significance is twofold: it shows that nature's power to comfort is not limited to pleasant images, and it emphasises the theme that even negative or overlooked elements can bring positive change. The "dust of snow" from these dark symbols becomes a symbol of unexpected grace.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about dealing with a bad day?
entries.answer: The poem teaches us to stay open to small moments of grace even on our worst days. The speaker begins the day full of regret, but a tiny natural incident — snow falling from a tree — completely changes his outlook. The lesson is that we do not need dramatic events to recover from gloom; small pleasures, a breath of fresh air, a glimpse of nature, can save our day. The poem also teaches us not to judge things by their appearance: the crow and the hemlock, symbols of darkness, become instruments of joy. If we remain receptive to the world around us, we will find that even the smallest and darkest moments can bring light, and that a single change of mood can redeem an entire day.

entries.prompt: Explain the use of contrast in the poem.
entries.answer: The poem is built on contrast. There is the contrast between the speaker's initial gloom and his final lightness of heart. There is the contrast between the dark, negative symbols — the crow and the hemlock tree — and the bright, positive outcome. There is the contrast between the tininess of the event ("dust of snow") and the greatness of its effect (saving a whole day). Finally, there is the contrast between the coldness of snow and the warmth it brings to the speaker's heart. These contrasts create the poem's depth: Frost shows that smallness can carry greatness, darkness can bring light, and a moment can change a day. The poem's power lies in these gentle oppositions.

entries.prompt: How does Frost's choice of words contribute to the effect of the poem?
entries.answer: Frost's word choice is simple, precise and musical. Words like "dust", "shook", "saved" and "rued" are short and crisp, matching the lightness of the snow and the brevity of the moment. The alliteration ("saved some part", "Has given my heart") creates a soft, falling rhythm that mirrors the falling snow. The word "dust" is deliberately modest — it makes the snow seem tiny and insignificant, which heightens the miracle of its effect. The word "rued" carries old-fashioned weight, capturing the speaker's genuine regret. Every word works to compress the poem's meaning into eight short lines, showing Frost's mastery of the lyric form: the smaller the words, the larger the effect.

entries.prompt: Why is the poem called "Dust of Snow" rather than "The Snow"?
entries.answer: The title "Dust of Snow" is carefully chosen. "Dust" suggests something tiny, fine and easily overlooked — a mere sprinkling of snow, not a heavy fall. This smallness is central to the poem's theme: it is precisely because the incident is so trivial that its effect is so remarkable. Calling it simply "The Snow" would imply a grand, obvious event, but the poem is about the power of the insignificant. The word "dust" also connects the snow to the earth, giving it a homely, grounded quality. The title thus prepares the reader for the poem's central idea: the smallest dust of snow, from the darkest of trees and birds, can save a day — and perhaps more.

entries.prompt: Meaning of the poem
entries.answer: The poem is a short philosophical meditation on the end of the world. Some people, the speaker says, believe the world will end in fire, while others believe it will end in ice. The speaker has experienced desire, which he compares to fire, and so he agrees with those who favour fire as the agent of destruction. But he also knows what hate feels like — its coldness — and he thinks that ice would also be sufficient to destroy the world. The poem thus weighs two forces — desire and hatred, fire and ice — and finds both equally capable of bringing destruction.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves from a general, almost scientific question — how will the world end? — to a deeply personal reflection. The speaker first reports the opinions of others ("Some say..."), then reveals his own experience of desire and hate. The fire of desire and the ice of hatred are shown to be twin dangers: one burns, the other freezes, but both destroy. In just nine lines, Frost compresses a meditation on human passion and destruction, ending with the quiet, almost understated conclusion that ice "would suffice" — hatred alone is enough to end everything. The movement is from the cosmic to the personal, and the tone from speculation to certainty.

entries.prompt: Desire and hatred as destructive forces
entries.answer: The central theme is the destructiveness of human emotions. Fire symbolises desire — burning, consuming, uncontrollable — and ice symbolises hatred — cold, hardening, paralysing. Frost suggests that the world is destroyed not only by cosmic forces but by human passions: our desires and our hatreds are the fires and ices that can end everything. The poem warns that both extremes — hot passion and cold hate — are equally dangerous.

entries.prompt: The end of the world and human responsibility
entries.answer: The poem links the question of cosmic destruction to human behaviour. The "world" that ends in fire or ice can be read both literally (the planet) and metaphorically (civilisation, relationships, peace). Frost suggests that the forces that will destroy the world already live within us — desire and hate. The theme implies that humanity holds the key to its own end, and that controlling our passions may be the only way to save the world.

entries.prompt: The speaker
entries.answer: The speaker is a reflective, experienced person who weighs two opinions about the end of the world. He reveals that he has known desire ("I have tasted of desire") and understands hatred, giving his words the weight of experience. He is not dogmatic: he does not reject the ice of hatred outright but admits it too would suffice. His balanced, measured tone suggests wisdom and a clear-sighted understanding of human nature.

entries.prompt: Structure and rhyme
entries.answer: The poem is only nine lines long, written in an unusual and irregular rhyme scheme (ABA ABC BCB). The compact form mirrors the compactness of the idea: a whole philosophy of destruction in nine lines. The irregular rhyme gives the poem a conversational, thoughtful quality, as if the speaker is thinking aloud. The brevity of the poem also echoes the finality of the subject — the end of everything requires few words.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone is calm, speculative and quietly ominous. The speaker begins conversationally ("Some say..."), as if discussing a casual theory, but the subject — the end of the world — gives the calmness an edge of menace. The final lines, "And would suffice", are delivered with chilling understatement: the speaker is not alarmed but matter-of-fact, which makes the warning more powerful. The mood moves from curiosity to a sober recognition of human destructiveness.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem uses elemental imagery: fire and ice, heat and cold, burning and freezing. Fire symbolises desire — intense, consuming and passionate; ice symbolises hatred — cold, fixed and paralysing. The symbols are universal and immediate: everyone understands the danger of fire and ice. Frost uses these natural images to make an abstract idea (human passion destroying the world) concrete and vivid. The contrast between the two elements creates the poem's tension, and the symbols remain relevant because desire and hatred are eternal human traits.

entries.prompt: ANAPHORA
entries.answer: The repetition of "Some say" at the beginning of consecutive lines ("Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice.") emphasises the two opposing opinions and gives the poem a balanced, debate-like structure. The anaphora makes the reader weigh fire against ice, desire against hatred.

entries.prompt: SYMBOLISM
entries.answer: Fire symbolises desire — hot, consuming, destructive; ice symbolises hatred — cold, paralysing, deadly. The two elements stand for the two great human passions that, according to Frost, are capable of ending the world. The symbolism is the heart of the poem's meaning.

entries.prompt: PERSONIFICATION
entries.answer: Fire and ice are spoken of as if they were active agents capable of ending the world: fire "would end" the world, ice "is also great". By treating these elements as forces with intent, Frost gives them the power of living enemies — desire and hatred — rather than mere natural phenomena.

entries.prompt: METAPHOR
entries.answer: The world's end in fire is a metaphor for destruction by desire, and the end in ice is a metaphor for destruction by hatred. The poem as a whole is an extended metaphor: cosmic destruction stands for the ruin wrought by human passions on individuals and civilisations alike.

entries.prompt: UNDERSTATEMENT
entries.answer: The final line, "And would suffice", is a masterful understatement. After imagining the destruction of the world by fire and ice, the speaker dismisses hatred with a quiet, modest word — but the effect is chilling: hatred alone is enough to end everything. The understatement heightens the poem's power.

entries.prompt: CONTRAST (FIRE VS ICE)
entries.answer: The poem is structured on the contrast between fire and ice — heat and cold, passion and indifference, desire and hatred. The contrast gives the poem balance and forces the reader to consider which force is more dangerous. Frost's answer is ambiguous: both are enough, suggesting that human destructiveness comes in opposing but equally deadly forms.

entries.prompt: RHYME SCHEME (ABA ABC BCB)
entries.answer: The irregular rhyme scheme gives the poem a conversational, musing quality. The rhymes (fire/desire, ice/suffice) link key words, binding the symbols together, while the irregularity prevents the poem from becoming sing-song, keeping the tone serious and thoughtful.

entries.prompt: What do "some say" about the end of the world?
entries.answer: Some say the world will end in fire, while others say it will end in ice. The speaker reports both opinions at the start of the poem.

entries.prompt: Why does the speaker agree with those who favour fire?
entries.answer: The speaker agrees with those who favour fire because he has "tasted" desire, which is hot and consuming like fire. His own experience of desire convinces him that fire is a powerful agent of destruction.

entries.prompt: What do fire and ice symbolise in the poem?
entries.answer: Fire symbolises desire — burning, consuming passion — and ice symbolises hatred — cold, paralysing ill-will. Both are human emotions capable of destroying the world.

entries.prompt: Why does the speaker think ice would also be enough?
entries.answer: The speaker knows what hatred feels like — its coldness — and he understands that hatred, like ice, can destroy slowly but surely. He therefore concludes that ice "would suffice" to end the world.

entries.prompt: How many lines does the poem have?
entries.answer: The poem has only nine lines — one of the shortest poems Frost wrote.

entries.prompt: What is the rhyme scheme of "Fire and Ice"?
entries.answer: The rhyme scheme is ABA ABC BCB, an irregular pattern that gives the poem a conversational, thoughtful quality.

entries.prompt: Which device is used in "Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice."?
entries.answer: Anaphora — the repetition of "Some say" at the beginning of consecutive lines, emphasising the two opposing views.

entries.prompt: What does the poet imply about human passions?
entries.answer: The poet implies that human passions — desire and hatred — are as destructive as the elemental forces of fire and ice, and that they are capable of bringing about the end of the world.

entries.prompt: What is the central idea of the poem "Fire and Ice"?
entries.answer: The central idea of the poem is that human emotions are destructive forces capable of ending the world. Frost uses fire and ice as symbols of desire and hatred. Fire represents hot, consuming desire — the passion that burns through everything; ice represents cold, hardening hatred — the indifference that freezes everything. By weighing both, the speaker concludes that either is sufficient for destruction. The poem can be read on two levels: literally, as a meditation on how the world might end (by fire or ice), and metaphorically, as a warning that human passions — unchecked desire and hatred — can destroy civilisation, relationships and peace. The message is that humanity carries the seeds of its own destruction within its heart.

entries.prompt: Why does the poet say that both fire and ice are dangerous?
entries.answer: The poet says both fire and ice are dangerous because they represent the two great destructive passions of humanity: desire and hatred. Fire — desire — destroys quickly and violently: it burns, consumes and cannot be easily controlled. Ice — hatred — destroys slowly and quietly: it freezes, hardens and paralyses, but its effect is just as deadly. The speaker, having tasted desire, can testify to its power; having known hatred, he understands that cold hatred is "also great". Frost thus shows that destruction comes in opposite forms — heat and cold, passion and indifference — and that neither is to be underestimated. The poem warns that whether the world ends in a blaze of desire or a freeze of hatred, the result is the same: ruin.

entries.prompt: Value question: What lesson does the poem teach us about controlling our emotions?
entries.answer: The poem teaches that unchecked emotions — desire and hatred — can destroy not only individuals but the whole world. Fire and ice are forces of nature, but Frost uses them to represent the passions within us: desire that burns out of control and hatred that freezes our hearts. The lesson is that we must learn to control these emotions before they control us. Desire, when unchecked, consumes relationships, resources and peace; hatred, when nursed, hardens the heart and leads to cruelty and war. The poem urges us to practise moderation, understanding and forgiveness, because the same passions that can end the world can also end our personal peace, our friendships and our humanity. Self-control is not weakness — it is survival.

entries.prompt: Explain the use of symbolism in the poem.
entries.answer: The poem is built entirely on symbolism. Fire is not merely the element but a symbol of desire — intense, consuming and passionate, the force that drives people to excess. Ice is not merely the element but a symbol of hatred — cold, fixed and paralysing, the force that hardens hearts and divides people. Frost uses these elemental symbols because they are universal and vivid: everyone knows the danger of fire and ice, just as everyone knows the danger of desire and hatred. The "world" itself can be read symbolically — as the planet, as civilisation, or as an individual's peace of mind. The symbolism makes an abstract philosophical idea concrete, and it gives the poem its timeless power: desire and hatred will always exist, and their destructive potential remains as real as fire and ice.

entries.prompt: How does Frost achieve so much meaning in such a short poem?
entries.answer: Frost achieves remarkable depth in nine lines through compression and implication. He uses elemental symbols (fire, ice) that carry immediate meaning, saving words. He uses the anaphora "Some say" to present both views economically and dramatically. He reveals personal experience — "I have tasted of desire" — in a single line, giving the poem authority without explanation. The understated ending, "And would suffice", implies more than it states: the reader understands that hatred alone can destroy the world without Frost spelling it out. The irregular rhyme scheme keeps the tone natural, and the contrast between fire and ice creates tension in a few words. Every word works; nothing is wasted, which is exactly what makes the poem so powerful.

entries.prompt: Do you think desire or hatred is more destructive? What does Frost suggest?
entries.answer: Frost deliberately does not choose a winner. He first aligns himself with those who favour fire, because he has tasted desire — suggesting desire's power. But he immediately adds that ice — hatred — "is also great", and ends with the chilling understatement that ice "would suffice". The structure suggests that both are equally capable of destruction, just in different ways: desire destroys by burning, fast and spectacular; hatred destroys by freezing, slow and silent. Frost's balanced treatment implies that it is futile to ask which is worse — both are deadly. The reader is left to consider their own experience: the fires of unchecked ambition and the ices of grudges and prejudice are both capable of ruining lives and worlds.

entries.prompt: Meaning of the poem
entries.answer: The poem is a miniature masterpiece of just six lines, in which the poet compares fog to a cat. The fog comes "on little cat feet" — silently, softly and stealthily. It sits looking over the harbour and the city on "silent haunches", and then it moves on. The poem captures the essence of fog: its silent arrival, its quiet presence and its mysterious departure. Like a cat, the fog comes without warning, stays without noise and leaves without explanation.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves through three phases of the fog's presence: arrival, presence and departure. The fog "comes" — silently, on little cat feet. It "sits looking" — over the harbour and the city, on silent haunches, watching the world below. Then it "moves on" — leaving as quietly as it came. The movement of the poem mirrors the movement of a cat and of fog: a slow, silent, almost imperceptible progress. In just six lines, Sandburg captures the whole life of the fog — its coming, its watching and its going — and the poem's brevity itself echoes the fog's quiet, fleeting nature.

entries.prompt: Nature as a quiet presence
entries.answer: The central theme is the quiet, mysterious presence of nature. The fog does not announce itself; it arrives silently, watches silently and departs silently. The poem celebrates the gentleness of nature — fog as a soft, silent visitor that disturbs nothing. The theme suggests that nature's power is often quiet and subtle, and that we must pay attention to notice its movements.

entries.prompt: The brevity and mystery of natural phenomena
entries.answer: The poem captures the fleeting, mysterious nature of fog. It comes and goes without explanation, like a cat that appears and vanishes. The poem's brevity — just six lines — mirrors the brevity of the fog's visit. The theme celebrates the mystery of natural phenomena: we cannot control them, fully understand them or keep them; we can only observe and appreciate them while they last.

entries.prompt: The fog
entries.answer: The fog is the poem's subject and, through the extended metaphor, its character. It is silent, stealthy and cat-like: it comes on little cat feet, sits looking over the harbour and city on silent haunches, and then moves on. The fog is not a violent force but a quiet presence — a watcher that observes the world below without interfering. Its character is that of the cat: independent, mysterious and self-contained.

entries.prompt: The cat (implied)
entries.answer: The cat exists through the extended metaphor of the poem. Sandburg never mentions a cat directly, but every description of the fog evokes one: the "little cat feet", the sitting posture, the "silent haunches", the way it "moves on" without a sound. The cat is the ideal comparison for fog because cats move silently, watch quietly and come and go as they please — exactly like fog. The cat gives the fog personality, making a natural phenomenon feel alive.

entries.prompt: Structure and form
entries.answer: The poem is extremely compact: six lines in two stanzas, written in free verse. The first stanza is a couplet — "The fog comes / on little cat feet." The second stanza is a quatrain — "It sits looking / over harbor and city / on silent haunches / and then moves on." The form's brevity is deliberate: like the fog itself, the poem is brief, quiet and unassuming. The poem is often described as a hokku-like verse, echoing the Japanese haiku tradition of capturing a moment of nature in a few words.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone of the poem is quiet, gentle and observant. The poet does not dramatise the fog or moralise about it; he simply watches and describes, like the fog itself watching the harbour. The mood is calm and contemplative — the reader, like the poet, is invited to pause and notice the silent arrival and departure of the fog. The poem's quietness is its power: it asks us to slow down and observe the small, quiet movements of the natural world.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem's imagery is simple and precise: the fog on cat feet, sitting over the harbour and city on silent haunches. The images combine the natural (fog, harbour, city) with the animal (cat, feet, haunches), creating a hybrid picture of fog as a living creature. The fog symbolises the quiet, mysterious forces of nature — and perhaps the fleeting, unnameable moments of life that come, watch and pass. The harbour and city below the fog symbolise the human world, watched over by nature's silent presence.

entries.prompt: EXTENDED METAPHOR
entries.answer: The entire poem is one extended metaphor: fog is compared to a cat throughout — its coming "on little cat feet", its sitting "on silent haunches" and its "moving on" like a cat. The extended metaphor gives the fog personality and makes a natural phenomenon feel alive and familiar.

entries.prompt: PERSONIFICATION
entries.answer: The fog is given animal, almost human actions: it "comes", "sits", "looks" and "moves on". By treating the fog as a living creature, the poet makes its presence felt and gives its silent movement a kind of intentionality — the fog is not a thing but a being.

entries.prompt: ALLITERATION
entries.answer: The poem is rich in alliteration: "little cat feet", "sits looking", "silent haunches", "harbor and city". The repeated sounds — the soft "s" and "c" — mimic the soft, silent movement of fog and cat, giving the poem a whispery, stealthy quality.

entries.prompt: IMAGERY
entries.answer: The poem creates vivid sensory images: fog moving on little cat feet, sitting over the harbour and city, crouching on silent haunches. The images are visual and tactile — we can see and almost feel the soft, silent presence of the fog as it watches the world below.

entries.prompt: ENJAMBMENT
entries.answer: The lines flow into one another without punctuation, as in "It sits looking / over harbor and city". The unbroken flow mirrors the continuous, seamless movement of the fog — it does not stop or pause, just as the lines of the poem do not.

entries.prompt: HOKKU-LIKE FORM
entries.answer: The poem's brevity and focus on a single moment of nature echo the Japanese haiku tradition: six lines capturing the essence of fog in a few precise images. The form's minimalism mirrors the fog's quietness — nothing is wasted, and everything is exactly as it needs to be.

entries.prompt: What is the fog compared to in the poem?
entries.answer: The fog is compared to a cat — it comes "on little cat feet", sits "on silent haunches" and moves on, just like a cat.

entries.prompt: How does the fog come, according to the poet?
entries.answer: The fog comes "on little cat feet" — silently, softly and stealthily, without any announcement, just like a cat padding along.

entries.prompt: What does the fog do while it is present?
entries.answer: The fog sits looking over the harbour and the city, on silent haunches — a quiet watcher observing the world below.

entries.prompt: How does the fog leave?
entries.answer: The fog "moves on" — it departs as silently and mysteriously as it came, without explanation.

entries.prompt: How many lines does the poem have?
entries.answer: The poem has just six lines in two stanzas — a couplet and a quatrain — making it one of the shortest poems in the collection.

entries.prompt: Why is the cat a suitable comparison for fog?
entries.answer: A cat is a suitable comparison because cats move silently, watch quietly and come and go as they please — exactly like fog, which arrives, observes and departs without a sound.

entries.prompt: What is the form of the poem?
entries.answer: The poem is written in free verse — no regular rhyme or metre — with a compact, haiku-like structure that matches the brevity of the fog's visit.

entries.prompt: What is the central idea of the poem?
entries.answer: The central idea is the quiet, mysterious, fleeting presence of fog — a silent natural visitor that comes, watches and moves on, like a cat.

entries.prompt: How does the poet create the comparison between fog and a cat?
entries.answer: The poet creates the comparison through an extended metaphor that runs through the entire poem. The fog "comes" — like a cat padding in on "little cat feet". It "sits looking / over harbor and city" — like a cat perched and watching. It sits "on silent haunches" — a phrase that evokes the crouching posture of a cat. Then it "moves on" — like a cat that has had enough and quietly departs. Every word works to build the comparison: the feet, the sitting, the haunches, the silent watching, the unannounced departure. The comparison is so complete that the fog becomes a cat — a living creature with personality and presence. The extended metaphor gives the fog mystery and life, making a natural phenomenon feel familiar, watchful and independent.

entries.prompt: Why does Sandburg call the fog's feet "little cat feet"?
entries.answer: Sandburg calls the fog's feet "little cat feet" to capture the way fog arrives: silently, softly and stealthily. A cat's feet are padded — they make no sound — and the fog, like a cat, steals in without any warning or noise. The word "little" adds a touch of gentleness: this is not a threatening force but a soft, quiet presence. The phrase also creates a striking visual image: the fog does not sweep in like a storm but pads in softly like a kitten. The comparison is perfect because both fog and cats move in ways that are silent, careful and almost magical — you notice them only when they are already there.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about observing nature?
entries.answer: The poem teaches us to pay attention to the quiet movements of nature. Fog is easy to ignore — it is silent, slow and undramatic — but Sandburg shows that even such a quiet phenomenon has a beauty and a mystery worth noticing. The poem asks us to slow down, watch and observe: the fog comes, sits looking over the harbour and city, and moves on. If we do not look, we will miss it entirely. The lesson is that the natural world is full of quiet wonders — the way fog pads in on little cat feet, the way a cat watches from its haunches — and that attentiveness is a virtue. In a noisy world, the poem invites us to appreciate silence, subtlety and the small moments of beauty that pass us by when we are not looking.

entries.prompt: How does the form of the poem reflect its subject?
entries.answer: The form of the poem mirrors its subject in several ways. The poem is extremely short — just six lines — reflecting the brief visit of the fog: it comes, stays a moment and moves on. The free verse, with its flowing enjambment, mirrors the continuous, seamless movement of the fog. The compact, haiku-like structure captures a single moment of nature in a few precise images, just as the fog itself is a single, fleeting phenomenon. The poem's quietness — its lack of drama, noise and ornament — mirrors the fog's silence. Even the line breaks seem to pad along like cat feet, moving the reader forward without any jolt. Form and content are perfectly matched: the poem is as brief, quiet and mysterious as the fog it describes.

entries.prompt: Why is the fog described as "looking over harbor and city"? What does this suggest?
entries.answer: The fog "sits looking over harbor and city" — the phrase suggests that the fog is a silent watcher, perched above the human world, observing it from its quiet heights. The harbour and the city are the centres of human activity — ships, work, movement — and the fog looks down on them from a detached, almost contemplative position. The image suggests the indifference or transcendence of nature: the fog comes, watches the human world going about its business, and moves on, unaffected. It also creates a striking contrast: the busy harbour and city below, and the silent fog above, watching. The phrase gives the fog a kind of consciousness — a watcher, not a participant — which deepens the poem's mystery and reinforces the theme of nature as a quiet, observing presence.

entries.prompt: What makes the poem an example of imagist poetry?
entries.answer: The poem is a classic example of imagist poetry, a movement that Sandburg helped to lead. Imagist poetry presents a single, precise image in few words, without moralising, explanation or ornament. "Fog" does exactly this: it offers one extended image — fog as a cat — and lets the image speak for itself. The poem does not tell us what fog means or what we should feel about it; it simply shows the fog coming, sitting and moving on, and trusts the reader to respond. The language is plain and exact ("little cat feet", "silent haunches"), and every word is essential. The poem's brevity, its focus on the image, and its refusal to moralise make it a perfect example of imagism: a whole world of feeling and meaning condensed into six quiet lines.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The invisible man
entries.answer: The story begins with two boys at a London inn who see fresh, wet footprints appearing one by one on the pavement — as if made by an invisible man. The footprints lead to a house, and the boys summon the landlady. Soon the town is full of wild stories of an "invisible man". The narrator reveals the truth: a scientist named Griffin had discovered how to make the human body invisible — by turning it to a state so transparent that light passes through it. But Griffin was a brilliant yet lawless man, who used his discovery only for his own ends: he set fire to his landlord's house and fled, invisible.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The theft at the shop
entries.answer: Griffin, invisible and penniless, needed money and warm clothes. He wandered the streets of London until he found a shop that sold theatrical items — masks, wigs and costumes. He broke in at night, stole clothes and food, and slept on a pile of quilts. But in the morning, the shopkeeper heard noises in the shop, and Griffin had to flee again, throwing off the clothes he had stolen, so that he ran out of the shop completely invisible, chased by the angry shopkeeper and his assistant.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — Dr Kemp and the story
entries.answer: Griffin then headed for the village of Iping, where he took a room at the local inn, appearing as a stranger wrapped in bandages, with dark glasses and a false nose — for he was still invisible, and had to cover every part of his face. The villagers were suspicious of the odd guest. Griffin robbed the vicar's house for money and blamed the innkeeper's wife. Eventually, the villagers grew hostile, and Griffin, in a rage, revealed his invisibility to the doctor who had been called, and fled. He then went to the house of Dr Kemp, a former fellow scientist, and told him the whole story — and his plan: to begin a "reign of terror" over the world.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The hunt begins
entries.answer: Kemp was horrified by Griffin's murderous ambition and quietly sent a note to the police. When Griffin discovered the betrayal, he attacked Kemp, but the police arrived, and a great hunt for the invisible man began — men with dogs and lanterns searching the countryside. The story ends with the hunt in full swing, the invisible man still at large, and Kemp awaiting his help — a moment of high suspense. (The story is an excerpt from H.G. Wells's novel "The Invisible Man".)

entries.prompt: The misuse of science
entries.answer: The central theme is the danger of science divorced from morality. Griffin makes a brilliant scientific discovery — invisibility — but uses it for crime, theft and a "reign of terror". The story warns that knowledge without conscience is a weapon: science must serve humanity, not the selfish ends of its discoverer.

entries.prompt: Power and its corrupting influence
entries.answer: The theme of power and corruption is central. Invisibility gives Griffin absolute power over others — he can steal, spy and attack unseen — and this power corrupts him completely. He moves from petty theft to arson to open terrorism, declaring he will rule the world through fear. The story shows that unchecked power, without accountability, turns even brilliant men into monsters.

entries.prompt: Alienation and human nature
entries.answer: Griffin's invisibility cuts him off from humanity: he cannot be seen, touched or trusted, and he must cover himself with bandages and clothes, becoming a strange and frightening figure to every community he enters. The theme of alienation runs through the story — invisibility, the ultimate symbol of not belonging, drives Griffin to loneliness, rage and cruelty.

entries.prompt: Griffin
entries.answer: Griffin is the brilliant but lawless scientist of the story. He discovers how to make the human body invisible, a feat that could have been a gift to science and humanity. But he is a "lawless person": he uses his discovery to burn down his landlord's house, steal food, clothes and money, rob a vicarage and terrorise whole villages. He is ruthless, egotistical and consumed by his vision of power — he dreams of a "reign of terror" over the world. Yet he is also a tragic figure: invisible, homeless, covered in bandages, he is utterly cut off from human society. Griffin represents the dangers of genius without conscience.

entries.prompt: Dr Kemp
entries.answer: Dr Kemp is a scientist and Griffin's former acquaintance, living in the village of Burdock. When the desperate, invisible Griffin appears at his house, Kemp listens to his story — and his monstrous plan. Unlike Griffin, Kemp remains bound by human feeling and duty: he is horrified by the idea of a reign of terror and quietly alerts the police. When Griffin discovers the betrayal, Kemp faces his rage alone, but the police arrive in time, and the hunt for the invisible man begins. Kemp represents the responsible scientist — one who, faced with the misuse of science, chooses society and morality over the brilliant madman.

entries.prompt: The Iping villagers
entries.answer: The villagers of Iping are ordinary, suspicious country folk. When the bandaged stranger arrives at the inn, they are curious and uneasy; when the vicarage is robbed, suspicion turns to accusation; and when Griffin finally reveals his invisibility in a rage, they are terrified. Their reaction — from gossip to hostility to flight — shows how an "invisible" outsider is treated by a community: with fear, rumour and rejection. They are the ordinary world against which Griffin's extraordinary power is measured.

entries.prompt: Science must serve humanity
entries.answer: The story teaches that science without ethics is dangerous. Griffin's discovery could have been used for good, but he used it for theft, terror and violence. The lesson is that knowledge and power must be guided by conscience, and that scientists are responsible for how their discoveries are used.

entries.prompt: Power corrupts without accountability
entries.answer: Griffin's invisibility gives him power over others while freeing him from accountability — no one can see him, so no one can stop him. The story shows that power unchecked by responsibility corrupts the wielder and terrorises society. The lesson: freedom and power must go hand in hand with responsibility.

entries.prompt: What did the two boys see on the pavement?
entries.answer: They saw fresh, wet footprints appearing one by one, as if made by an invisible man.

entries.prompt: How did Griffin make himself invisible?
entries.answer: He discovered how to turn the human body transparent by making it absorb and refract light completely, so light passes through it.

entries.prompt: What was Griffin's first crime?
entries.answer: He set fire to his landlord's house to destroy his own belongings and fled, invisible.

entries.prompt: What did Griffin do at the theatrical shop?
entries.answer: He broke in at night, stole clothes and food, and slept there, until the shopkeeper's discovery forced him to flee naked and invisible.

entries.prompt: How did Griffin appear at the inn at Iping?
entries.answer: He appeared as a stranger wrapped in bandages with dark glasses and a false nose, hiding his invisible body.

entries.prompt: How did Griffin get money at Iping?
entries.answer: He robbed the vicar's house, and the blame fell on the innkeeper's wife.

entries.prompt: Who was Dr Kemp?
entries.answer: He was a scientist and Griffin's former fellow student, living in Burdock, to whom Griffin told his story.

entries.prompt: What plan did Griffin share with Kemp?
entries.answer: He planned to begin a "reign of terror" and rule the world through fear, using his invisibility.

entries.prompt: How did Griffin misuse his scientific discovery?
entries.answer: Griffin's discovery — how to make the human body invisible by making it transparent to light — was a scientific marvel, but he used it purely for crime and selfish ends. Penniless and invisible, he first set fire to his landlord's house to destroy his possessions, then stole clothes, food and money from shops. He robbed the vicar's house in Iping and let the blame fall on an innocent woman. When his disguise of bandages failed and the villagers grew hostile, he revealed himself in a rage and fled. Finally, he went to Dr Kemp with a monstrous plan: to begin a "reign of terror" over the world. Instead of using his genius to benefit humanity, Griffin turned it into a weapon of theft, fear and violence — the classic warning about science divorced from conscience.

entries.prompt: Describe Griffin's appearance and behaviour at Iping. Why were the villagers suspicious?
entries.answer: At Iping, Griffin was invisible, so he had to cover every inch of his body: he arrived at the inn as a stranger wrapped in bandages, wearing dark glasses and a false nose, his hat pulled low. He kept to himself, and the villagers were deeply suspicious of the odd visitor. Their suspicions grew when the vicarage was robbed: the money disappeared without a trace, and Griffin, in his rage and carelessness, even made accusations against the innkeeper's wife, whom he blamed for the theft he himself had committed. When the doctor came to examine his strange injuries, Griffin lost his temper completely, revealed his invisibility and fled. The villagers' suspicion was natural — a hidden, mysterious stranger with unexplained behaviour and unexplained crimes could only frighten a small, trusting community.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about the relationship between science and morality?
entries.answer: The story teaches that science and morality must never be separated. Griffin is a scientific genius — he achieves what no one else has, the invisibility of the human body. But he is also "lawless": he uses his achievement for arson, theft, robbery and finally terrorism. The discovery itself is neutral; it is Griffin's character that makes it evil. The lesson is that scientists bear responsibility for their discoveries, and that knowledge without conscience becomes a danger to society. The story also warns about the corrupting effect of power: invisibility frees Griffin from accountability, and that freedom turns him into a monster. A true scientist, like Dr Kemp, uses knowledge within the bounds of morality — Kemp chooses society and alerts the police. The story's message remains relevant: every great discovery must be governed by ethical responsibility, or it becomes a reign of terror.

entries.prompt: How does the story create suspense?
entries.answer: The story creates suspense from its very first lines: two boys see wet footprints appearing on the pavement with no one to make them — a mystery that immediately seizes the reader. The narrator then withholds the explanation, letting wild rumours of an "invisible man" sweep the town, building curiosity. Griffin's escape from the shop adds action and danger: the invisible man fleeing the angry shopkeeper and assistant is vivid and thrilling. At Iping, suspense grows with each suspicious detail — the bandaged stranger, the robbed vicarage, the false accusation — and climaxes when Griffin's invisibility is revealed in front of the frightened villagers. Finally, the story ends on a peak of tension: Griffin's plan of a reign of terror, his betrayal of Kemp, and the great hunt with dogs and lanterns across the countryside. The excerpt closes mid-hunt, leaving the invisible man at large — a perfect cliffhanger.

entries.prompt: Compare the characters of Griffin and Dr Kemp.
entries.answer: Griffin and Dr Kemp are both scientists, but they embody the two faces of science. Griffin is a genius — he discovers invisibility, an unprecedented achievement — but he is lawless and selfish. He uses his discovery for arson, theft and terror, dreams of a "reign of terror", and treats other people as obstacles. He is brilliant, bold and utterly without conscience. Kemp is also a man of science, but he remains anchored to human values: when Griffin appears at his house with his monstrous plan, Kemp is horrified rather than tempted. He does not join his former friend; he quietly alerts the police, risking his own safety. Where Griffin's brilliance is self-serving, Kemp's knowledge is used in the service of society. Their confrontation — the mad genius against the responsible scientist — is the moral core of the story, showing that science is judged by the character of those who wield it.

entries.prompt: Stanza-wise meaning
entries.answer: The poem is a dialogue about love and beauty. In the first stanza, the speaker tells Anne Gregory that no young man will ever love her for herself alone: any man who is "thrown into despair" by her beauty will love her for her golden hair, not for her true self. He uses the striking image of her hair as "honey-coloured ramparts" — the walls of a fortress that keep her true self hidden. In the second stanza, Anne replies that she can get a hair-dye and set her colour right — she can make her hair black, brown or carrot-coloured, and then she can be loved for herself alone. In the third stanza, the speaker reports what an old religious man declared the night before: that he had found a text proving that only God could love Anne Gregory for herself alone and not for her yellow hair. The poem thus concludes that human love is attracted by outward beauty, and that only divine love sees past appearances.

entries.prompt: Overall movement of the poem
entries.answer: The poem moves through three voices: the young man's warning, Anne's practical reply, and the old religious man's conclusion. The young man insists that men love only beauty — Anne's yellow hair, not her inner self. Anne responds with a childlike practicality: she can dye her hair, and then no one will love her for it. The old religious man delivers the final judgment: only God can love Anne for herself alone. The movement is from the personal to the universal, and from human love to divine love. The poem ends with a quiet, humbling truth: human beings are attracted by appearances, and unconditional love — love for the self alone — belongs only to God.

entries.prompt: Outer beauty versus inner self
entries.answer: The central theme is the contrast between outer beauty and the inner self. The poem argues that human beings are attracted by appearances — the young man loves Anne's yellow hair, not Anne. The theme questions the shallowness of human love and celebrates the idea of the inner self, which deserves to be loved for what it is, not for how it looks. The poem's message is that beauty is only a surface, and that the true person lies beneath it.

entries.prompt: The nature of love: human and divine
entries.answer: The poem distinguishes between human love and divine love. Human love, the poem suggests, is conditioned by appearances — it loves the hair, the face, the beauty. Divine love is unconditional: only God loves the self alone, without any attraction to outward form. The theme is humbling and profound: it suggests that unconditional love is the highest ideal, attainable only by the divine, and that human love, however sincere, is always touched by the attraction of the visible.

entries.prompt: Anne Gregory
entries.answer: Anne Gregory is the young woman of the poem — beautiful, with honey-coloured yellow hair. She is practical and spirited: when told that men love only her beauty, she does not despair but proposes a solution — she can dye her hair. Her reply shows a young woman who is not vain but aware of the world's ways, and who longs to be loved for herself. She is the object of the poem's reflection on beauty, and her youthful practicality contrasts with the old man's spiritual wisdom.

entries.prompt: The young man (first speaker)
entries.answer: The first speaker is a young man addressing Anne Gregory. He speaks from experience and perhaps cynicism: he warns Anne that no man will ever love her for herself alone, because men are so struck by her beauty that they cannot see beyond it. His image of the honey-coloured ramparts suggests that beauty is a fortress that hides the true self. He represents human love in its imperfection — attracted by the visible, unable to reach the inner person.

entries.prompt: The old religious man
entries.answer: The old religious man appears in the third stanza, where the poet reports his words. He has found a text — probably from scripture — proving that only God can love Anne Gregory for herself alone, and not for her yellow hair. He represents divine wisdom: the understanding that unconditional love, which sees past appearance, is the privilege of God alone. His brief appearance gives the poem its final, universal meaning.

entries.prompt: Structure and rhyme
entries.answer: The poem is written in three stanzas, each ending with the refrain "And not your yellow hair" (with slight variation in the second stanza: "And not her yellow hair" in the third). The rhyme scheme is regular (abcbdb), giving the poem a song-like, ballad quality. The dialogue structure — a young man speaking, Anne replying, and the poet reporting an old man's words — gives the poem the movement of a dramatic conversation, and the refrain binds the stanzas together musically and thematically.

entries.prompt: Tone and mood
entries.answer: The tone of the poem is reflective and gently philosophical. The young man's words are frank and slightly sad; Anne's reply is spirited and practical; the old man's conclusion is serene and wise. The mood moves from a worldly observation about love to a spiritual reflection on the nature of unconditional love. The refrain — "and not your yellow hair" — recurs like a theme in music, binding the poem's reflections into a single, quiet meditation on beauty and love.

entries.prompt: Imagery and symbolism
entries.answer: The poem's central image is the "honey-coloured ramparts" — Anne's yellow hair imagined as the walls of a fortress. The image is striking: beauty becomes a defensive structure that hides the true self from lovers. The ramparts symbolise the power of beauty to obscure the person within. The hair itself symbolises outward beauty — the surface that attracts human love — while "yourself alone" symbolises the inner self, the true person. The poem's imagery is spare but resonant, carrying the full weight of its reflection on appearance and reality.

entries.prompt: METAPHOR
entries.answer: The poem's central metaphor is "honey-coloured ramparts" — Anne's golden hair is compared to the fortified walls of a city. The metaphor suggests that her beauty is a fortress that keeps lovers out, hiding her true self behind its walls. The image is both beautiful and sad: the very thing that attracts love also prevents it.

entries.prompt: SYMBOLISM
entries.answer: The yellow hair symbolises outward beauty — the visible surface that human beings love. "Yourself alone" symbolises the inner self, the true person. The ramparts symbolise the barrier that beauty creates between the person and the world. The poem's symbolism distinguishes between what is seen and what is real.

entries.prompt: REFRAIN
entries.answer: The line "And not your yellow hair" is repeated at the end of each stanza (with "her" in the final stanza), functioning as a refrain. The repetition drives home the poem's central idea — that no human love can see past the yellow hair — and gives the poem its musical, ballad-like structure.

entries.prompt: DIALOGUE FORM
entries.answer: The poem is structured as a dialogue: the young man speaks, Anne replies, and the poet reports the old religious man's words. The dialogue form dramatises the poem's theme, presenting different perspectives on love and beauty, and it gives the poem the movement of a conversation rather than a monologue.

entries.prompt: REPETITION
entries.answer: Key words and phrases recur throughout the poem: "love you for yourself alone", "not your yellow hair", "never shall a young man". The repetition emphasises the poem's central idea and creates a rhythm of insistence, as if the speaker must convince Anne of the truth he has learned.

entries.prompt: RHYME SCHEME (ABCBDB)
entries.answer: Each stanza follows the abcbdb rhyme scheme, with the final "b" line rhyming with "hair" — the refrain. The regular, song-like rhyme gives the poem the quality of a ballad, and the recurring rhyme on "hair" ties the poem's sound to its theme of beauty.

entries.prompt: ALLITERATION
entries.answer: The poem uses alliteration for musical effect, as in "honey-coloured", "young man", "yellow hair". The repeated sounds give the verse a soft, flowing quality that suits the poem's gentle, reflective tone.

entries.prompt: What does the young man tell Anne Gregory at the start of the poem?
entries.answer: The young man tells Anne that no young man will ever love her for herself alone — men who are thrown into despair by her beauty will love her only for her yellow hair.

entries.prompt: What is the image used for Anne's hair?
entries.answer: Anne's hair is described as "honey-coloured ramparts" — the golden walls of a fortress. The image suggests that her beauty is a barrier that hides her true self from lovers.

entries.prompt: How does Anne propose to be loved for herself?
